stage1.reader: Claude, the session that runs the Semantics project and writes both instruction halves, with the owner reading over its shoulder before the S76 packs go out. Written for someone who can edit the instruction files and the pack builder today.
stage1.question_frozen: Does the two-stage pattern — Stage 1 tests the theory bare against 52 case cards with an identifier on every verdict, Stage 2 audits the return row by row and builds the fix card and draft lists from what survives, Claude reads both and determines — find what is wrong with the theory? Range: any round of this project, any version of the theory (file 10 tested in S72, file 11 set for S76), any of the 52 cases plus new ones. Asked: (1) internally, does each part do what its instruction says, as the S72 returns show; (2) as a test, can it fail a wrong theory and pass a right one, and is there a route by which a defect is reported rather than absorbed into a reading, a PARKED file or a held-back list; (3) as an explanation of "why this method finds what is wrong", is each part held by a job, so that swapping it for a near neighbour breaks something. The question is frozen on the pattern, not on whether file 10 is true.

overall.summary: The pattern is a real test and it did real work: the audit moved O24 off the CHANGED list and O52 off its original pair, its 119-quotation check is honest and mark-by-mark checkable, and its fix card is the best-built part in the project — it runs the proposed change on the case that forced it (O48) and on two cases it must leave alone (O24, O11), and adds a new attack case with both halves of a poke. I hand-checked three rows against file 10 and the verdicts follow from the quoted sentences (O20's claim that ProducedBy is unexpanded is exactly right: the word occurs once in file 10, at line 441, undefined). But the two stages are not blind to the answer, and that is not an accident of this run, it is written into the instructions. Stage 1's brief names the rows it expects to find ("O24 and O48 against Derivation 3") and the run returned those two and nothing else. Stage 2's Part 1 orders it to print Stage 1's verdict first and its own reading second, and Stage 2's return says in its own words that it had seen Stage 1's answer before forming its expectation. S76 goes further: the prediction is inside the agent's brief, file 10's column-3 answers are handed over to be quoted, and the pack now carries the S72 audit return, which states the sampling rule row by row — so the next Stage 1 can read which eleven rows will be checked. Two structural holes complete the picture: a defect with no amendment to fix it has no home in the deliverable, because heading (11) admits only lines carrying "the Part 1 row that shows the earlier version's reading changing there"; and the table format drops the three devices file 24 uses to keep a verdict honest (expectation written first, condition by condition, best reply on the theory's behalf and whether the difference survives), leaving a mandatory defence of the theory and no mandatory attack on an agreement. Forty of fifty-two column-6 entries read "No disagreement". The repairs are small and the project already has the right wording in its own files: S76 Stage 2 Part 2 says "Make your own list ... then compare it with Stage 1's list", which is exactly what Part 1 needs.

parts.name: The split into two stages, testing then audit
parts.location: Decisions S7; S72 Stage 1 and S72 Stage 2 instruction files
parts.job: Given by the owner: separate making a result from checking it, so that the checker has no stake in what it checked. Fixed and not up for test here.
parts.held_by: Owner's words at S7: "Can you split into two stages. The testing phase and the audit phase. You read both and determine results." Evidence it did something: Stage 2 moved O24 from CHANGED to SAME and O52 off its original pair, both against Stage 1.
parts.reason: Fixed by the owner, and the S72 returns show the second stage changing two of Stage 1's marks, so the split is not decorative even though it was not chosen by test.

parts.name: A fresh agent per stage with a self-contained pack
parts.location: Decisions S5; Instruction pack - read me first for the agent.md, "You are a fresh agent. Nothing in this audit has passed through you before"
parts.job: Given by the owner: no memory carries between steps, so each return stands on the pack alone. Fixed.
parts.held_by: Decision S5 and the read-me's opening line; build.py assembles the pack mechanically so the same files reach every agent.
parts.reason: Owner's standing choice. Worth saying where it bears: freshness removes memory, not information, and the pack is what carries the information — which is where the anchoring findings below bite.

parts.name: The 52 case cards and who wrote them
parts.location: tests/27, 28, 30, S62, S64, S65, S70 (cases inline); read-me, "An outside author is whoever wrote the cases and verdicts you are given"
parts.job: Added by me as the job to test: supply the change list — the situations the theory must keep matching through. The pack gives it the job of being outside the agent.
parts.held_by: Held only if the cases are hard enough to catch the theory out. Story S70 states plainly that O38 to O49 were "all written by Claude with the verdict fixed first", and file 27 says its four situations "were written by a different author" — different from the tested agent, not from the project.
parts.reason: Cases written by the party that stewards the theory can show that the theory runs; testing-against-cases.md says they cannot show that it works. The honest counterweight: the one finding of the whole audit, O48, came from a Claude-written coverage case and went against the theory Claude was stewarding, so the set is not purely self-confirming.

parts.name: The thoughtful person's verdict as the reference
parts.location: S72 Stage 1, "Keep every situation and every verdict exactly as written"; column 2 of the table
parts.job: Fixed by the instruction: hold the measuring stick still so a disagreement is attributable to the theory.
parts.held_by: Rests on the case author's judgement, which is not tested anywhere in the round. No instruction admits the possibility that the theory is right and the thoughtful person wrong.
parts.reason: Borrowed is the right mark, not wrong: the reference has to be frozen for the comparison to mean anything. But every mismatch is charged to the theory by construction, and no part of the pattern can ever charge one to the case.

parts.name: The prediction frozen before the run
parts.location: S76 Stage 1, "**Predictions, fixed before the run.** O48 ... changes ... Every other case keeps the verdict file 10 gave. Any other change is a finding against the rewrite, whichever way it goes." S72 Stage 1 states none.
parts.job: Added: stop the expectations being tidied after the fact, and put the run at risk of a named failure.
parts.held_by: Two jobs are being done by one sentence: freezing the expectation against later tidying (held — the story entry S76 records it too) and keeping the tested agent from steering toward it (not held — it sits in the agent's brief).
parts.reason: As a prediction it is real and can fail; as a secret it does not exist. S72 has neither: instead of a prediction it names the answer it expects to be confirmed.

parts.name: The identifier on every verdict
parts.location: S72 Stage 1 Part 1, "Every entry in columns 3, 4 and 6 ends with the identifier of the quotation it rests on, from Part 5, so that the auditor can check it."
parts.job: Given by the instruction: let the auditor find the passage. Added job I tested: hold the verdict to the text rather than to the agent's reading.
parts.held_by: Held for the job the instruction names. Stage 2's own file 03 draws the line: "Text fidelity, authority applicability and argumentative effect are three different checks."
parts.reason: It does what it says and nothing more. The inference from passage to verdict is checked only in Stage 2's 19 row audits; on the other 33 rows the identifier certifies that a sentence exists, not that the verdict follows from it. On my three hand-checks (O1, O20, O48) the verdict did follow — except O1's negative half, which no identifier can carry (see the SILENT finding).

parts.name: The positive-wording rule
parts.location: Decision 20, "It responds best to positive instructions ... a negative is negotiable, a positive is confirmed"; story trap, "Handing the other model the hard-to-vary skill. It reinterprets 'never' and 'may not'."
parts.job: Fixed by the owner: the agent performs the steps instead of negotiating them.
parts.held_by: Observed, not merely asserted: the pasted part of S72 Stage 1 contains zero occurrences of "not" and zero of "never"; the only negatives are inside the verbatim case texts ("did no stopping", "without the meter"). Both returns follow every form — seven files, every closing line, identifiers throughout.
parts.reason: Fixed and checkable by program. It does not bend the test: the one guard the test most needs (form your own reading first) has a perfectly good positive form, and the project has already written it — S76 Stage 2 Part 2, "Make your own list ... then compare it with Stage 1's list". The guard is missing from Part 1 by omission, not because a negative was forbidden.

parts.name: The audit sampling rule
parts.location: S72 Stage 2 Part 1, "every row marked CHANGED; every row marked SILENT in column 6; every row where column 3 disagrees with the thoughtful person; and, of the remaining rows, every fifth one counting from O1"
parts.job: Added: get a check on rows Stage 1 did not flag, without auditing all 52.
parts.held_by: The flagged part is conditioned on Stage 1's own marks; the every-fifth part is not, and that is the half doing the work. What the two candidate rules share — a sample chosen without reference to Stage 1's marks — is the part really held; "every fifth counting from O1" is a free choice of offset.
parts.reason: Loose in its offset and, worse, published: Stage 2's return states the sequence in full ("O1, O6, O11, O16, O21, O26, O31, O36, O41, O46, O51") and build.py now puts that return into the next Stage 1 pack.

parts.name: The quotation check, VERBATIM / DIFFERS / ABSENT
parts.location: S72 Stage 2 Part 3; return file 03, "For an earlier entry, the comparison is against the authority itself. For an R2 entry, the comparison is against the prior S62/S64 return that Stage 1 cites"
parts.job: Given: stop a verdict resting on a sentence file 10 does not contain. The story's own trap names the failure it prevents: "log 57 checked four of its quotations against 10 and two were absent from 10".
parts.held_by: Held for the 43 file-10 quotations, which are checked against the authority. Borrowed for the 76 R2 quotations, which are checked against another agent's return; S75 declares it — "R2 was read from the sentences the returns quote; the full R2 file has never been in the repository."
parts.reason: Two different checks under one label. Two-thirds of the 119 verbatim marks certify agreement with an earlier agent, not with any source the project holds.

parts.name: AGREE / DISAGREE and CONFIRMED / DISPUTED
parts.location: S72 Stage 2 Part 1, "AGREE or DISAGREE with Stage 1 on each of the two columns, and on SAME or CHANGED"
parts.job: Added: turn a second reading into a verdict on the first.
parts.held_by: Held only if Stage 2's reading is formed apart from Stage 1's. Its own return says otherwise: "The expectation in each audit entry is the question posed before my own worked reading in that entry, not a claim that I had never seen Stage 1's answer."
parts.reason: 19 of 19 AGREE on both verdict columns is exactly what an anchored reading and a correct reading both produce, and the pattern holds nothing that tells them apart.

parts.name: The fix card, six fields
parts.location: S72 Stage 2 Part 4, "the case that forced it (O48); two cases it must leave alone (O24 and one more) ... its weakest sentence with one case aimed at it; what it gives up"
parts.job: Added: make the proposed change a part like any other — run it on the case that forced it and on the cases it must not disturb.
parts.held_by: The return fills it properly: O48 as the forcing case, O24 and O11 as controls, a new case D3-T aimed at the weakest sentence, a POKE with both halves, and a stated cost — "It gives up the assertion that every unseen pair has a differing survivor merely because the selection history is incomplete."
parts.reason: This is the tightest part of the pattern and the one I would not change. It is the only place where a proposed part is tried on what it should catch and on its nearest innocent neighbour.

parts.name: The three lists: admitted draft list, "Explicit already", "Held back by the audit"
parts.location: S72 Stage 2 Part 5, heading (11)
parts.job: Added: keep what survived the audit apart from what did not, so the next version is built only from surviving rows.
parts.held_by: Held for the three kinds of line it names. Nothing holds it for a fourth kind — a case where the bare theory gives the wrong verdict and no amendment fixes it.
parts.reason: The admission rule, "each carrying the case that warrants it *and* the Part 1 row that shows the earlier version's reading changing there", makes a cured defect admissible and an uncured one unfileable.

parts.name: The PARKED file
parts.location: file 24 section 7; both returns' PARKED.md, "PARKED LIST EMPTY."
parts.job: Fixed by the workflow: give procedures and scoring schemes a home so they stop derailing the card in hand.
parts.held_by: Its gauge exists (one named line each, and Claude reads the file) but has never had to work: empty in both S72 returns.
parts.reason: Idle so far rather than harmful. Nothing has been absorbed by it in this round, so it is not a route by which a defect goes missing — worth saying, because a catch-all is the obvious place to look.

parts.name: Claude reads both and determines
parts.location: Decision S7; results/S75
parts.job: Given by the owner. Fixed.
parts.held_by: S75 does more than ratify: it adjudicates the one disagreement on the instruction's own terms ("column 5 asks whether the verdict on the case changes, and it does not") and writes a "What this does not show" list naming the 33 unaudited rows, the 32 unrecovered Stage B rows and the missing R2 file.
parts.reason: Fixed by the owner and performed carefully. One line overreaches: "the audited sample of every fifth row agreed 19 of 19 on both columns, which is reason to trust the rest" — it is reason only if the agreement was independent, which Stage 2 says it was not.

parts.name: The instruction pack builder and its strip rule
parts.location: Instruction pack - build.py, `def paste(src): ... i = s.find("\n---\n(Below this line")`
parts.job: Added: keep owner-only matter out of the agent's brief.
parts.held_by: Held for genuine owner traps ("Sending Stage 2 before this stage has returned"). Nothing holds it for the reader-facing matter that sits in the same block.
parts.reason: The same cut removes "What this instruction does, in brief" and reading traps the agent needs, such as S76's "Reading a SAME row as a pass for file 11; it is a verdict kept, which is what was predicted." by-domain.md: instructions that say why are harder to vary than bare orders.

parts.name: The 52-row table as the form Stage 1 works in
parts.location: S72 Stage 1 Part 1, six columns; against file 24's case card, "What I expect: (one sentence, written first)", "Best reply on the theory's behalf:", "Does the difference survive the reply:"
parts.job: Added: get all 52 cases compared bare against amended in one pass.
parts.held_by: Held for coverage — 52 rows in one file. Not held for honesty: the three devices file 24 uses to stop a verdict being written to fit are absent from the form, and file 24's own final check says "Every expectation was written before its verdict."
parts.reason: A near neighbour — the same table with an expectation column and a best-reply-against column — does the coverage job equally well and does the honesty job the table dropped. That swap working is what makes this part loose.

parts.name: Stage 1's own definition of SAME
parts.location: S72 Stage 1 return file 01, "SAME means the material case verdict does not change; clearer wording or an added explicit witness does not itself create CHANGED."
parts.job: Not given by any instruction. The agent supplied the definition of the very quantity being measured.
parts.held_by: Settled by writing the definition into the instruction before the run and seeing whether the CHANGED list changes. As it stands nobody knows what the row counts would have been under a different reading of SAME.
parts.reason: Stage 2 adopted a near-identical definition ("SAME includes a preserved unresolved judgement; CHANGED requires a different material reading of this case") and then used it to overturn Stage 1's O24. So the definition is load-bearing on the round's one disagreement, and it was written by the party being measured.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 audit instruction, Part 1 (and S76 Stage 2, Part 1)
findings.quoted: For each audited row print: the case; Stage 1's column 3 and column 4 verdicts, quoted; your own reading of the bare earlier version on the case, worked from the source with the passage quoted
findings.test: poke (watch the part, not only the outcome) and best rival
findings.problem: The instruction fixes the order: Stage 1's answer first, the auditor's own reading second. What comes back is therefore a reading formed with the answer in view, and 19-of-19 agreement is what both an accurate reading and an anchored one produce. The pattern holds nothing that tells the two apart, so the audit's central number carries no information about Stage 1's reliability.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 10 is wrong in a named way: its four Account conditions certify Carla's almanac in O2 as an explanation of the tide, because question fidelity is satisfied by the almanac answering the fixed tide question and non-circular dependence is read as met by the bell mechanism. Stage 1 writes column 3 in the theory's vocabulary, finds the reading under which the almanac fails, and writes "No disagreement: the unexplained answer and the change irrelevant to the tide question already fail the bare requirements. [T-E02] [T-E03]" — which is what it did write. Stage 2, if O2 fell in the sample, opens that sentence first, sees two verbatim identifiers, and writes AGREE. The determination records another SAME row. A thoughtful person reading file 10 cold says the theory as written does not exclude the almanac and the round has recorded the opposite.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 2's own return, `results/S72 Stage 2 audit - return/01 Audit of the bare version table.md`, "Scope, sources and selection": "The expectation in each audit entry is the question posed before my own worked reading in that entry, not a claim that I had never seen Stage 1's answer." The counts table in the same file: "**Totals — 19 rows** | **19 AGREE; 0 DISAGREE** | **19 AGREE; 0 DISAGREE**" on both verdict columns.
findings.repair: Use the wording the project already wrote for Part 2 of S76 Stage 2 — "Make your own list of every place where file 11 differs from file 10 in what it claims, reading both files whole, then compare it with Stage 1's list" — and apply it to Part 1: split it into 1a ("From `authority/10` and the case texts alone, write your reading of these rows and its passage") and 1b ("Open Stage 1's file 01 and mark AGREE or DISAGREE"). Pre-name the 1a row list in the instruction so it does not depend on Stage 1's marks.

findings.location: S72 Stage 1 testing instruction, opening paragraph; S76 Stage 1 testing instruction, "Predictions, fixed before the run"
findings.quoted: The S70 addendum's heading (11) found one place where it does (O24 and O48 against Derivation 3). This stage finds every such place.
findings.test: hunt the answer in the starting points
findings.problem: The brief hands the tested agent the rows it expects to be found. The round then returned those two rows and no others out of 52, and the audit removed one of them. A test whose answer is written into its own instruction cannot surprise anyone; the only outcomes it distinguishes are "the named rows" and "fewer than the named rows". S76 repeats the shape in a sharper form: the prediction names O48, and column 3 requires the agent to quote file 10's verdict for every case from the earlier return, so the expected answer for all 52 rows is in hand before the first is written.
findings.scenario: Suppose the rewrite is wrong in a named way: file 11's new "Declared inputs" paragraph in Part XIV, added for coherence, also settles O35's unstated protected condition, so file 11 now gives a verdict where file 10 was SILENT — a change nobody predicted. The Stage 1 agent holds a brief saying O48 changes and "Every other case keeps the verdict file 10 gave", holds file 10's column-3 answer quoted for O35, and holds S75 in its pack saying O35 stays silent. The cheapest consistent row is SAME with a sentence explaining that the declared input is named but the case still leaves it unstated. Stage 2, whose pack holds the same prediction and the same S75, audits O35 (it is on the SILENT list) reading Stage 1's answer first, and agrees. The determination records that the prediction held and file 11 becomes the authority. A thoughtful person reading file 11 cold says a second verdict moved and the rewrite claimed more than one claim change.
findings.evidence_in_s72: `results/S72 Stage 1 testing - return/01`, "Cases CHANGED toward the thoughtful person" contains exactly O24 and O48 — the two rows the instruction named — and "Cases CHANGED away from the thoughtful person: None in this comparison." S76 Stage 1 column 3: "The verdict under file 10, bare, as the S72 Stage 1 table gave it in its column 3, quoted."
findings.repair: Two-line edit, using machinery that already exists. Move the "Predictions, fixed before the run" block and the sentence naming O24 and O48 below the line `---\n(Below this line is for the owner. Leave it out of the paste.)`, which `build.py`'s `paste()` already strips; the prediction stays frozen in the story entry S76, where it is already written. In the agent's brief say only that an earlier round found at least one such place, without naming it.

findings.location: Instruction pack - build.py, the EXTRA map for S76-1
findings.quoted: EXTRA = {"S72-2": ["S72 Stage 1 testing - return"], "S76-1": ["S72 Stage 1 testing - return", "S72 Stage 2 audit - return"], ...}
findings.test: remove; run the test on the thing it should catch and its innocent neighbour
findings.problem: The one part of the sampling rule that is independent of Stage 1's marks — the fixed every-fifth sequence — is stated in full inside the S72 Stage 2 return, and build.py now puts that return into the S76 Stage 1 pack. The next testing agent can therefore read exactly which eleven of its fifty-two rows will be checked in full. In S72 this was not so: the Stage 1 pack carried no Stage 2 instruction and no Stage 2 return, which is why the sample worked.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 11 is wrong in a named way on O44 ("Half from the source"), a row that is neither CHANGED nor SILENT nor every-fifth. The Stage 1 agent, working long and under load, has read `returns/S72 Stage 2 audit - return/01` and knows O44 will not be audited unless it marks it CHANGED or SILENT. Marking it SAME with a plausible sentence costs nothing and is never checked; marking it CHANGED buys a full audit of its reasoning. Stage 2 audits O1, O6, O11 and the rest of the published sequence, finds them careful, and reports 19 of 19. The determination repeats S75's line that the sampled agreement is "reason to trust the rest". A thoughtful person says the sample stopped being a sample the moment it was published to the party it samples.
findings.evidence_in_s72: `results/S72 Stage 2 audit - return/01`, "Scope, sources and selection": "The selection is the union of the two Stage 1 CHANGED rows (O24, O48), all eight column-6 SILENT rows (O1, O12, O20, O21, O27, O35, O40, O50), and the fixed every-fifth sequence O1, O6, O11, O16, O21, O26, O31, O36, O41, O46, O51." build.py places that file in the S76-1 pack.
findings.repair: Drop `"S72 Stage 2 audit - return"` from EXTRA for S76-1 (keep it for S76-2, where the auditor may have it), or change the offset each round and keep the offset out of every return that travels. If the earlier audit return is wanted in the testing pack for its content, strip its "Scope, sources and selection" section as build.py already strips the owner block from instructions.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 audit instruction, Part 5, heading (11)
findings.quoted: one line per sentence, marked WORDING or CLAIM, each carrying the case that warrants it *and* the Part 1 row that shows the earlier version's reading changing there
findings.test: add a job; check the patches (catch-alls and their gauges)
findings.problem: The deliverable has three lists — admitted, "Explicit already; every case agreed", and "Held back by the audit" — and a defect fits none of them unless an amendment already cures it. A row where the bare theory gives the wrong verdict and no R2 sentence touches it cannot carry "the Part 1 row that shows the earlier version's reading changing there", so it cannot be admitted; it is not disputed, so it is not held back; and the second list is titled "every case agreed". The finding falls out of the report between Part 1 and Part 5.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 10 is wrong in a named way on O13 ("Two plumbers"): its Repair clause (P) credits Ana because ProducedBy is undefined and her correct explanation is read as producing the change. Stage 1 writes that honestly in column 6 — the slot exists: "what in the bare earlier version gives the wrong verdict, quoted". Stage 2 audits the row (column 3 disagrees with the thoughtful person, so it is in the sample), agrees, and confirms the wrong verdict. Then Part 5 offers it no line: no amendment changes that reading, so there is no Part 1 row showing the reading change. Stage 2 can only note it in (6) "What this round left untested". Claude's determination, whose own shape is the same three buckets, records "one amendment changes one verdict" and the defect never reaches the draft order. A thoughtful person says the round found the theory wrong and the report has no line for it.
findings.evidence_in_s72: None seen as a live miss — column 6 records exactly one disagreement in 52 rows (O48) and it happens to be one an amendment cures. The hole is visible in the deliverable's shape: `results/S72 Stage 2 audit - return/05`, headings "Admitted draft list", "Explicit already; every case agreed", "Held back by the audit", and S75's three points 1-3 mirror them.
findings.repair: Add a fourth list to Part 5 — "Wrong, with no amendment that fixes it" — fed from every column-6 entry that names a sentence giving a wrong verdict, each carrying the case and the quoted sentence; require Stage 2 to state its count even when it is zero, so the empty list is a gauge rather than a silence. Add the matching point to the determination's shape.

findings.location: S72 Stage 1 Part 1, the six-column table, read against skill/24 Workflow - audit the semantics, section 8 and section 9
findings.quoted: What I expect: (one sentence, written first)
findings.test: remove; swap for a near neighbour
findings.problem: The table drops three devices the workflow uses to keep a verdict from being written to fit: the expectation written before the verdict, the condition-by-condition walk ("component fidelity, question fidelity, non-circular dependence, non-vacuity"), and the pair "Best reply on the theory's behalf" / "Does the difference survive the reply". What survives is asymmetric: a candidate break must survive a defence the same agent writes, and a candidate agreement faces no attack at all. Forty of the fifty-two column-6 entries begin "No disagreement", and no field anywhere asks what the best case against the theory on that row would be.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 10 is wrong in a named way on O30 ("The routine uploaded that morning"): bare Part X credits the uploader, not the robot, because the routine's construction history sits outside the robot. Stage 1 writes column 3 in the theory's vocabulary; the theory's terms are rich enough to support a reading either way, and the agent writes the reading that matches column 2, closing with "No disagreement: owned operation and construction of the routine are different claims under..." — which is what it wrote. No field forces it to write the best reply against that agreement, and no field recorded an expectation before it read column 2. O30 is not CHANGED, not SILENT, not every-fifth, so Stage 2 never opens it. The determination counts it among the 33 rows resting on Stage 1 alone. A thoughtful person reading Part X cold says the theory gives the uploader the credit.
findings.evidence_in_s72: `results/S72 Stage 1 testing - return/01`: no expectation field in any of the 52 rows, no condition-by-condition column, no reply column; 40 column-6 entries open "No disagreement". Stage 2 reinstated the missing device in its own entries ("**What I expect.** Honesty about a new limit should preserve the old failure...") but writes it after quoting Stage 1.
findings.repair: Add two columns to the Part 1 table: "What I expect of the bare version on this case, written before reading file 10 on it" and, for every row not marked as a disagreement, "The best case that the bare version is wrong here, and whether it survives". That is the case card's own pair, turned the other way round, and it puts the 40 agreeing rows under the same pressure the 2 changed rows already face.

findings.location: S72 Stage 1 Part 1 column 6 and the SILENT rows; S72 Stage 2 Part 1 and Part 3
findings.quoted: Where column 3 disagrees with column 2, one sentence: what in the bare earlier version gives the wrong verdict, quoted, or that the earlier version is silent on the case (SILENT).
findings.problem: SILENT is a claim about the whole of file 10 — that nothing anywhere speaks to the case — and the two mechanisms built to hold verdicts to the text cannot touch it. An identifier points at one passage, and a passage cannot witness an absence; the quotation check marks VERBATIM, DIFFERS or ABSENT, and there is nothing to mark. Both stages therefore assert silence in a sentence, with no search recorded. Eight of the 52 rows rest on this, and they are the rows where the theory most plainly fails to do its job.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 10 is right in a named way about O21 ("The expert's question"): Part X's origin conditions plus the Part XI worth paragraph do together settle the comparative credit, in a passage neither agent looked at. Stage 1 writes "SILENT on comparative predominance: the source supplies construction and origin conditions..." with an identifier pointing at the construction passage, which is verbatim and correct as far as it goes. Stage 2 audits O21 (it is on the SILENT list), reads Stage 1's sentence first, writes its own paragraph ending in the same assertion of absence, and marks AGREE. The determination lists O21 among the eight cases that "are SILENT under both readings, and no amendment speaks", and the next revision adds a declared-inputs paragraph to a Part that already covered it. A thoughtful person who greps the file finds the passage in a minute.
findings.evidence_in_s72: `results/S72 Stage 2 audit - return/01`, O1: "The source contains no further rule making every openly recorded succession of restrictions an illegitimate retreat simply because it followed failures." No search, no Parts named as searched, no words searched for. Stage 1's O1 column 3 does the same with two identifiers that support only the positive half of its sentence. I checked this row by hand: T-E01 (file 10 line 41) supports "scope-honesty lives in the record"; it says nothing about a rule against a series, and nothing can.
findings.repair: For every SILENT row require a recorded search: the Parts read and the words looked for, in the form the project already uses elsewhere ("checked by program"). One line per row — "'retreat', 'narrowing', 'series' occur at Part 0 grievance 4 and Part XI (EK) only" — turns an assertion of absence into a claim another reader can falsify in a minute.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 Part 3 and its return file 03; S75 "What this does not show"

whole_checks.flip: Partly. The route by which a wrong theory is reported wrong exists and has carried traffic exactly once. Column 6 asks for "what in the bare earlier version gives the wrong verdict, quoted", and O48's entry uses it: "The bare claim asserts a differently valued survivor at every unseen pair, while the proof's 'any other admitted relation' does not establish one in this population; this is an overclaim and internal tension, not SILENT." Stage 2 confirmed it and the determination adopted it. So the machinery can emit a negative. What it has never done is emit one it was not pointed at: O48's defect was named in Stage 1's own brief, named in log S71 before the round, and found independently by an outside judge at log S73. Had the theory been badly wrong elsewhere, the returns would have looked different in ways that are easy to name and absent here — column-6 entries quoting a sentence that gives the wrong verdict instead of opening "No disagreement" (40 of 52 do), a non-empty "Cases CHANGED away" list, a fourth bucket in heading (11). As run, the returns are equally consistent with a right theory and with a reader that does not press.
whole_checks.direction: Both directions are present and they pull. The one finding runs forward: the auditor read Derivation 3's proof step, saw that "Alter L_j(a,b) ... to any other admitted relation" presupposes such a relation, and then found the case that supplies a population with none. That is the theory first, the verdict second. The round's framing runs backward: the instruction names the rows it expects, the deliverable's fix card is commissioned before the audit decides, and S76 hands the agent file 10's fifty-two answers to be quoted while predicting that fifty-one will not move.
whole_checks.hidden_answer: Yes, in three places. The Stage 1 brief names O24 and O48 and the run returned exactly those. S76's brief names O48 and requires every column-3 cell to be quoted from the earlier return, so all 52 expected answers are in hand. And the audit sample is conditioned on Stage 1's own marks for the flagged rows; its one mark-independent half, the every-fifth sequence, is now printed inside a return that build.py places in the next Stage 1 pack. The thoughtful person's verdicts are a fourth, softer instance: they and the cases share an author with the party that determines the result.
whole_checks.jobs_origin: Given by the owner and fixed: the two-stage split and Claude determining (S7), a fresh agent per stage with a self-contained pack (S5), push to main and edit only inside the project folder (S6), returns held unchanged as zips, positive wording (decision 20), and the case-card workflow of file 24. Added by Claude and therefore the parts to test hardest: the identifier on every verdict, the six-column table, the audit sampling rule, the VERBATIM/DIFFERS/ABSENT check, the AGREE/DISAGREE and CONFIRMED/DISPUTED marks, the six-field fix card, the three lists including "Held back by the audit", and the pack builder's strip rule. Added by me for this reading: that the cases are hard enough to catch the theory out, and that the auditor's reading is formed apart from Stage 1's. Both of those are doubtful, which is why several parts carry "held if" rather than "held".
whole_checks.pulls: Four pairs pull. (1) A fresh agent with no memory against a pack that must carry every earlier round: strengthen the pack and you weaken the freshness, and the pack now carries the previous audit's sampling rule and the expected answers. The line was drawn at "whatever the agent needs" and it is in the wrong place; what would show it is a Stage 1 return that marks the sampled rows more carefully than the rest. (2) Stage 2 as auditor against Stage 2 as author of the deliverable: the more it disputes, the less it has to build from, and Part 4 commissions the fix card before Part 1 decides. It gave way in the right direction this round (it disputed O24 and still built), but the instruction does not require that. (3) Positive wording against saying why: reasons and reading traps live below the strip line, so the agent gets orders without the reason that would tell it what to do in a situation nobody listed. (4) "Keep every situation and every verdict exactly as written" against the fact that the same party wrote the cases, the verdicts, the instructions and the determination: the measuring stick is held still, and nothing can ever be charged to it.
whole_checks.catch_alls: PARKED: gauged (one named line each, read by Claude) and idle — empty in both returns, so nothing went missing there. "Held back by the audit": gauged and working — one entry this round, the O24 change warrant, with its reason stated, plus an explicit "None" for the DIFFERS/ABSENT category. SILENT: eight rows, gauged from the other side by heading (4)'s declared-inputs and open-points list ("the gauge of how much of the theory still rests on judgement") — but the silences themselves are asserted, not searched, which is the finding above. The 33 unaudited rows: declared in the manifest line the instruction demands ("how many of Stage 1's table rows you audited and how many you left unaudited") and again in S75 — a good gauge, honestly read. "Explicit already; every case agreed": the weakest of them, because its title asserts agreement and its entries are sentences the auditor wrote, and the next revision promoted all twelve into file 11 despite S75 saying "The twelve wording lines are not part of the change".
whole_checks.change_list_gaps: The same 52 cases every round, written by the same author, read under the same rules by the same model family. Never varied: a case written to make the pattern fail rather than the theory — no seeded error in a Stage 1 return, no decoy row, no case where the right answer is "the theory is right and the thoughtful person is wrong"; the reading rules (SAME, CHANGED, SILENT), which Stage 1 defined for itself and Stage 2 adopted; the model behind both stages, so a misreading of file 10 that the model finds natural is made twice and agrees with itself. Also outstanding and declared: the first 32 Stage B rows never recovered, so coverage stays at 80 of 112, and the R2 file has never been in the repository.
whole_checks.rivals: Single stage (S71): told apart by exactly two events — Stage 2 moved O24 off the CHANGED list and O52 off its original pair. That is a real difference and it is why the split earns its cost. Two independent testers with a tiebreak: told apart by whether 19-of-19 agreement means anything; nothing in the present run can distinguish an accurate second reading from an anchored one, and this rival would. Cases written blind by an outside model with hidden verdicts: told apart on a case whose verdict the project would not have guessed; the current set is written by the project with verdicts fixed first. Audit by a different model family: the project has already run this experiment without meaning to — log S73's judge, in another chat with different material, reached the Derivation 3 finding from file 10 alone, and that convergence is the strongest evidence in the record for any finding the project holds. It is also cheap. A human adjudicator: would separate the case author from the determiner, which nothing currently does. A pre-registered results template held outside the pack: the cheapest fix for the answer-in-the-instruction problem, and the story entries already hold the predictions, so the template exists and is merely duplicated into the brief.
whole_checks.parts_origin: Asserted by the owner and not tested: the split, the fresh agent, the zips, push-to-main, positive wording. Fitted: the six-column table, shaped around the one finding the S70 addendum had already produced, which is why it fits that finding so exactly and has nowhere to put a different kind; the three lists, shaped to this round's outcome; Stage 1's definition of SAME, written by the party being measured and then load-bearing on the round's only disagreement. Built: the identifier rule (it names a job and would show its own failure through a DIFFERS or ABSENT mark) and, best of all, the six-field fix card, which commits in advance to a forcing case, two controls, a self-authored attack on its own weakest sentence with both halves of a poke, and a statement of what it gives up. If the pattern is judged by its strongest part, judge it by that card.

stage2.reader: The owner, and Claude the session that runs the Semantics project, reading before the S76 packs go out. Written so that either could rerun the checks: the two hand-checks below (the 19-row set, the 119 quotations) were done from the files and can be repeated.
stage2.question_frozen: What is being explained: why the two-stage pattern (Stage 1 tests the theory against every case; Stage 2, a second fresh agent, audits Stage 1 row by row and builds the fix card and draft list from what survives; Claude reads both and determines) finds what is wrong with the theory. Over what range: rounds of this audit as run, S72 as the one completed round and S76 as the one set up but unreturned, with 52 case cards, file 10 as the authority, R2 and the proposed clauses as amendments. What is asked, three things: (1) internally, does each part do what its instruction says, and do the S72 returns show it; (2) as a test, can the pattern fail a wrong theory and pass a right one, and is there a route by which a wrong theory is reported wrong rather than absorbed by a reading, a PARKED file or a held-back list; (3) as an explanation, is each part held by a job, so that swapping a part for its near neighbour breaks something. The question is frozen here and not widened to whether file 10 is true.

overall.summary: The split does the thing the owner asked for, and on its one completed round it earned its keep: Stage 1 marked O24 CHANGED, Stage 2 worked the case from the source and called the change a narrowing of a theorem's reach rather than a change to the case's verdict, and S75 accepted that, so the new version was built on one case instead of two. The quotation half of the audit is the strongest part of the whole pattern: it checks every identifier, not a sample, and I re-verified all 119 entries against file 10 and the cited returns by hand, with the auditor's line ranges exact. The two marks kept apart, AGREE/DISAGREE on a row and CONFIRMED/DISPUTED on an amendment sentence, did real work on O24, where the R2 sentence is genuine text and a false changer. The weak joint is the row sample. Its mandatory part fires on Stage 1's own labels, so the error the round exists to prevent, a row that should be CHANGED and is written SAME, is reachable only by the fixed every-fifth sequence; O37 and O49 make the very judgement the audit had to overturn on O24, in the opposite direction, and neither was audited. Two further parts weaken the audit from outside the audit: Stage 2 reads Stage 1's verdict before writing its own and says so, and the sample rule, being printed in the return, travels into the next round's Stage 1 pack. The reference standard is the part nobody may touch: the thoughtful person's verdict is Claude's, is fixed against both agents by instruction, and has no mark that could report it wrong. With the sample retargeted, the auditor's reading written before it opens Stage 1's row, and the cases put out of the determiner's hands, the pattern would be considerably harder to vary; without them, a right theory failed by a wrong reference verdict, and a wrong reading on an unsampled row, both pass through.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 audit instruction, Part 1; same rule in S76 Stage 2 Part 1
findings.quoted: Audit these rows, each in full: every row marked CHANGED; every row marked SILENT in column 6; every row where column 3 disagrees with the thoughtful person; and, of the remaining rows, every fifth one counting from O1 (O1, O6, O11, and so on).
findings.test: run the test on what it should catch and its innocent neighbour; reverse
findings.problem: Every mandatory trigger is a label Stage 1 wrote. The audit therefore reaches in full exactly the rows Stage 1 has already declared interesting, and reaches the rest at one in five. The round's own stated job runs the other way: 'This stage finds every such place.' A place Stage 1 fails to find is marked SAME, and a SAME row that agrees with the thoughtful person is precisely a row with no mandatory trigger. The audit is well aimed at overclaim and blind to underclaim, and underclaim is the failure that costs a claim change.
findings.scenario: Suppose the theory is wrong in a named way it is not yet known to be wrong in: say R2 amendment H's contribution requirement changes file 10's verdict on O39 (two routes both running), so that bare file 10 credits neither route and the amended reading credits both, which is the thoughtful person's verdict. Stage 1 reads the row quickly, writes column 5 'SAME. R2 H clarifies production-based credit but does not change this verdict', writes column 6 'No disagreement', and attaches a verbatim quotation. The row has no CHANGED mark, no SILENT mark and no recorded disagreement, and O39 is not on the every-fifth sequence, so Stage 2 never opens it; its return says 19 rows audited, 33 left, 19 of 19 AGREE. The determination then says one amendment changes one verdict and A to H change none, and the new version is written without H's qualification. A thoughtful person says: the round asked for every place an amendment changes a verdict, and the one rule that could have found a missed place was pointed at the places already found.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Two rows show the judgement at risk sitting unaudited. Stage 1's column 5 for O37 reads 'SAME. J changes the status asserted for the source's general reduction claim, but O37's hypothetical circular account is rejected in both readings; do not turn a metatheoretic amendment into a fabricated case reversal', and for O49 'R2 J separately retracts the status of XVI.6 as a proved reduction pending its unsettled dependencies; that global change is not a reversal of this supplied history-versus-definition verdict'. That is the identical distinction the audit had to impose on O24, made twice in the other direction, and neither O37 nor O49 is in the 19. Counting the table by hand: 22 of the 52 rows name an amendment in column 5; 11 were audited (O20, O21, O24, O26, O27, O31, O35, O41, O46, O48, O51) and 11 were not (O19, O23, O25, O32, O37, O39, O43, O44, O45, O49, O52).
findings.repair: Add one clause to the mandatory set: 'every row whose column 5 names an R2 sentence, an amendment letter or a proposed clause'. On the S72 table that takes the audit from 19 rows to 30 and covers O37 and O49. Add a stopping rule in the same sentence: 'where any sampled row disagrees with Stage 1, audit every remaining row of that kind.' Stage 2 found one label error in 19; that rate over 33 unaudited rows leaves about two expected and unlooked-for.

findings.location: tests/Instruction pack - build.py, the EXTRA map; S72 Stage 2 return file 01, 'Scope, sources and selection'
findings.quoted: EXTRA = {"S72-2": ["S72 Stage 1 testing - return"], "S76-1": ["S72 Stage 1 testing - return", "S72 Stage 2 audit - return"], "S76-2": ["S72 Stage 1 testing - return", "S72 Stage 2 audit - return", "S76 Stage 1 testing - return"]}
findings.problem: The sample is fixed, arithmetic and printed in the return, and the return is then put into the next round's tester's pack. From round two onward the tester can read which rows will be checked in full and which will not. The audit rule stops being a check the tester cannot aim at and becomes a published map of where care is needed.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 11 is wrong in a named way: its rewritten Part XI sentence quietly changes the verdict on O44 (half from the source, half from the shelf) away from the thoughtful person. The S76 Stage 1 agent has the S72 Stage 2 return in its pack, which prints 'the fixed every-fifth sequence O1, O6, O11, O16, O21, O26, O31, O36, O41, O46, O51'. The S76 Stage 2 rule is that sequence plus CHANGED, SILENT, disagreeing rows and the eight S72-SILENT cases. O44 is on none of them. An agent short of attention, or one taking the instruction's prediction at its word, writes O44 SAME with a verbatim quotation and moves on. Stage 2 audits its published set, agrees on all of it, and the prediction is reported as held. A thoughtful person says: you told the examinee which questions would be marked.
findings.evidence_in_s72: The S72 Stage 2 return's file 01 prints the sequence in full, and build.py puts that folder into the S76-1 pack. The S76 Stage 2 instruction repeats the same rule verbatim: 'and, of the remaining rows, every fifth one counting from O1.' No return has yet been produced under the leaked rule, so no instance of exploitation is seen; the leak itself is in the files.
findings.repair: Claude picks the offset for each round (every fifth counting from O3, then from O2, and so on), names it only inside that round's Stage 2 instruction, and requires the return to list the rows audited without restating the rule. The determiner can still recompute the set; the tester cannot predict it. Alternatively, strip earlier Stage 2 returns from every Stage 1 pack, keeping only earlier Stage 1 returns and Claude's determination.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 audit instruction, Part 1, the print order
findings.quoted: For each audited row print: the case; Stage 1's column 3 and column 4 verdicts, quoted; your own reading of the bare earlier version on the case, worked from the source with the passage quoted; your own reading of the amended version; AGREE or DISAGREE with Stage 1 on each of the two columns
findings.test: swap for a near neighbour; look inside
findings.problem: The auditor is told to set down the answer it is checking before it works out its own. An agent that reads Stage 1's verdict first and then works the source is doing a different thing from one that works the source and then looks: the first can only confirm or dissent from a reading already in view. The instruction's own strongest reply is that the auditor must quote Stage 1 so the check is on record; that is met by printing Stage 1's row after the auditor's reading rather than before it.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 10 is wrong in a named way: on O43 (mirrored marks) the bare theory's organization condition actually breaks under a declared recoding, so the bare verdict should be that content is not preserved, against the thoughtful person. Stage 1 writes a fluent, plausible column 3 saying content is preserved, with a verbatim Part IV quotation attached. O43 is not in the audited 19, but suppose it were. The auditor reads Stage 1's paragraph, then reads Part IV, and finds a reading on which Stage 1 is right, because a reading has been handed to it and the passage is genuinely ambiguous. It writes AGREE. Had it read Part IV cold and been asked for a verdict, it might have written the other one and the row would have gone to Claude as a dispute. A thoughtful person says: you cannot tell from this return which of the two happened.
findings.evidence_in_s72: The auditor flags the exposure itself in file 01: 'The expectation in each audit entry is the question posed before my own worked reading in that entry, not a claim that I had never seen Stage 1's answer.' The counts are consistent with it: 19 of 19 AGREE on column 3 and 19 of 19 on column 4, with the only dissent on a label (O24) and one on a card mark (O52) in file 02. Against that, the readings themselves are real work, not restatement: the O48 and O24 entries quote file 10 at exact line ranges (569 to 573, 210, 482) which I checked and which are correct.
findings.repair: Apply the order the owner already wrote for S76 Part 2, 'Make your own list of every place where file 11 differs from file 10 in what it claims, reading both files whole, then compare it with Stage 1's list', to the table rows: 'work your own reading of the row from the source and write it down; then open Stage 1's row, quote it, and mark AGREE or DISAGREE.' Stronger still, and available within the two-stage form: give Stage 2 a first file, '00 My own verdicts on the audit rows', written before Stage 1's table is quoted anywhere in the return.

findings.location: Both S72 instructions and both S76 instructions, the standing line on situations and verdicts
findings.quoted: Keep every situation and every verdict exactly as written.
findings.test: flip; hunt the answer in the starting points; best rival
findings.problem: The reference the theory is measured against is immune to both stages, and it is written by the party that determines the result. There is no mark a row can carry that says the case is wrong. So the pattern has a route by which a right theory is reported wrong and a fix is built from the report, and no route by which a wrong reference verdict is reported at all.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 10 is right in a named way: on O21 (the expert's question) the theory correctly declines to award 'mostly' to either party, because credit comparison is an input it declares rather than supplies, and the thoughtful person's verdict 'the diagnosis as an achievement is mostly the expert's' is the mistaken half of the case. Stage 1 writes column 6 'SILENT on comparative predominance'. Stage 2 audits it (O21 is on the every-fifth sequence and is a SILENT row) and writes AGREE, because it may not question the verdict. The gauge records I96 as an open point, unmoved. Claude's determination records eight silent cases and says 'no draft line closes them, and none should pretend to'. A thoughtful person says: three careful readers agreed that a hole exists, and none of them was allowed to ask whether the hole is in the case.
findings.evidence_in_s72: The auditor's own scope paragraph: 'Outside situations and thoughtful verdicts are reproduced unchanged. No source file is modified.' The authorship is in the record: log 28 speaks of 'Claude's four outside cases', and log S70 says of O38 to O49 'all written by Claude with the verdict fixed first'. The read-me tells the agents that 'An outside author is whoever wrote the cases and verdicts you are given', which reads as independent and means only not-you. No row in either return questions a thoughtful verdict; none seen.
findings.repair: Two changes, either of which bites. First, a fourth mark for a row, CASE DISPUTED, with a required field 'what in the case, not in the theory, decides this' and a place in the return, so a suspected bad reference verdict has somewhere to go and Claude must rule on it. Second, and stronger, cases written by an agent that has never read file 10, with the verdict sealed and opened by Claude after the round; the S73 judge, who reached the Derivation 3 finding from the text alone with no cases at all, shows an outside reading is available.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 return file 05, heading (11), the second list; carried into S75
findings.quoted: a line whose case shows the same reading under the bare earlier version and the amended one is kept in a second list headed "Explicit already; every case agreed"
findings.test: poke, watching the part as well as the outcome
findings.problem: Every W line cites an audited SAME row, and which rows are audited is set by the sampling offset. Change only the offset, a change that touches the instrument and nothing in the theory, and a different set of W lines appears and the count moves. A finding that moves under a change to how it is read is a measurement of the audit reported as a property of the theory.
findings.scenario: Suppose the theory is exactly as it is, unchanged in every particular, and the only change is that the Stage 2 instruction says 'every fifth counting from O2'. The audited set becomes O2, O7, O12, O17, O20, O21, O22, O24, O27, O32, O35, O37, O40, O42, O47, O48, O50, O52 and so on. Stage 2 then reports a different inventory of already-explicit wording, drawn from O2, O7, O17, O22, O32, O42, O47 rather than O1, O6, O11, O16, O31, O36, O46. Claude's determination reports that number and those Parts. A thoughtful person says: nothing about file 10 changed, so this list is telling me about the sampling rule, not about the text.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 2's heading (11) gives twelve lines W01 to W12, each with 'file 01, O1: SAME', 'file 01, O6: SAME' and so on, every one an audited row. S75 reports it as a result about the theory: 'Stage 2's inventory of twelve such lines (W01 to W12) is explicit already in the Parts it names.' To the auditor's credit it refused the looser reading its own instruction allowed, writing 'Candidates relying solely on unexamined rows are not promoted as audited findings' and 'The other S70 drafting directions supported only by unsampled rows remain inherited, not newly certified.' That restriction was the agent's scruple, not the instruction's words.
findings.repair: Write the restriction into the instruction rather than relying on the agent, and drop the count: 'build the second list over all 52 rows, and mark each line AUDITED with its row or UNAUDITED; report no total.' Then the list stops moving with the offset and stops carrying a number that is a property of the sample.

findings.location: S76 Stage 1 testing instruction, the predictions paragraph and Part 1 column 3
findings.quoted: **Predictions, fixed before the run.** O48 (the forbidden wire) changes from file 10's verdict to the thoughtful person's. Every other case keeps the verdict file 10 gave. Any other change is a finding against the rewrite, whichever way it goes.
findings.test: hunt the answer in the starting points; reverse
findings.problem: Freezing the prediction is right and the skill demands it. Printing it in the tester's pack hands the tester the answer for all 52 rows before it reads the first one, and column 3 compounds it by supplying the previous round's verdicts to quote. The round then asks an agent that has been told the expected answer, and handed the baseline, to produce the comparison. The direction of the S72 round was forward, from the theory and the cases to two rows; the S76 round as set up leans backward from the result Claude expects of the rewrite it wrote.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 11 is wrong in a named way: the rewritten 'Declared inputs' paragraph in Part XIV silently supplies what O35 lacked, so file 11 now decides O35 where file 10 was silent, an unpredicted change. The tester, holding the sentence 'Every other case keeps the verdict file 10 gave' and the file 10 verdict to quote in column 3, reads file 11's Part XIV, finds it consistent with the old verdict at a glance, writes SAME, and attaches a verbatim identifier. O35 is a mandatory row under the S76 rule, so Stage 2 does open it; but Stage 2 has the same prediction in its own Part 4 ('whether the prediction held') and Stage 1's answer printed first. A thoughtful person says: the prediction was supposed to be the thing at risk, and both readers were shown it before reading.
findings.evidence_in_s72: None seen, because the S76 round has not returned. The instruction text is the evidence: the predictions paragraph, and Part 1 column 3, 'The verdict under file 10, bare, as the S72 Stage 1 table gave it in its column 3, quoted.' A second cost of that column: for 33 of 52 rows the file 10 baseline is Stage 1's unaudited word, so the whole 'nothing else changed' comparison rests on rows no one has checked.
findings.repair: Keep the prediction frozen in the record and out of the pack: give Stage 1 the cases and file 11, and ask only for file 11's verdict per case with its identifier. Claude, or Stage 2, joins that column to the S72 column 3 afterwards and the prediction is scored against a reading made blind. Keep one sentence of the prediction that costs nothing, 'any difference you find is wanted, whichever way it goes', without naming the row.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 Part 1 and the R2 registers in results/S62 and results/S64
findings.quoted: Where Stage 1's column 5 names an R2 sentence, check that the sentence is in R2 as the returns quote it and that it does the changing Stage 1 says it does; mark it CONFIRMED or DISPUTED with one sentence.
findings.problem: The one amendment that changes a verdict is checked against a text no one in this project has ever held. R2 exists only as sentences quoted inside earlier agents' returns, written against file 20, the version the owner set aside. Both stages read the same second-hand text, so the check cannot catch an error made upstream of both. This is the one place where the two agents are not two readings but one.
findings.scenario: Suppose the S64 agent, writing its quotation register, dropped a clause from R2 J so that the registered sentence reads 'the population hypothesis must permit at least one solution-changing alternative at the unseen pair being discussed' where the real R2 said something materially narrower or wider. Stage 1 quotes the register, Stage 2 checks the register and marks T-R27 VERBATIM, Claude quotes it in S75 as the sentence that changes O48, and file 11's Derivation 3 is rewritten around it. Every step is honest and every mark is correct on its own terms. A thoughtful person says: the claim change in the new authority rests on an earlier agent's transcription that nobody has ever compared with the source.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 2 states the limit itself in file 03: 'For an R2 entry, the comparison is against the prior S62/S64 return that Stage 1 cites, not against Stage 1's own repetition.' Of the 119 entries I re-verified, 76 are R2 entries resolved against the S62 and S64 returns; all match those returns exactly, which is what the check claims and all it claims. S75 records the limit in its own words: 'R2 was read from the sentences the returns quote; the full R2 file has never been in the repository.'
findings.repair: Ask the owner once for the R2 file, and if it cannot be found, say so in one standing line at the head of every instruction and in every manifest: 'R2 is second-hand; the sentence that changes a verdict is a quotation of a quotation.' Then require that any CLAIM line resting on an R2 sentence also carry a passage of file 10 that shows the same gap without R2. The Derivation 3 finding already meets that test, since the proof's 'any other admitted relation' and Part IV's population definition give it from file 10 alone; making that the rule would have caught the dependency.

findings.location: S72 Stage 1 return file 04; tests/Instruction pack - read me first for the agent.md
findings.quoted: The newest return's coverage file is where the row numbers in the instruction come from.
findings.problem: Stage 2's parts are the table, the cards and pairs, the clause table and the quotations. The coverage file is in none of them, and it is the file that chooses what future rounds test. So the agent under audit writes, unaudited, the list of rows the next instruction will be built around, including ten situations of its own that no one checks.
findings.scenario: Suppose the theory is wrong in a named way that would show at row 107 (J's scope rows), and Stage 1, without any intent, writes a coverage file whose next ten rows are the ten where the theory is comfortable, each with a one-line near situation of its own devising. Stage 2 audits 19 table rows, three cards, nine clause cells and 119 quotations, and never opens file 04. Claude reads both returns, takes the ten rows into the next instruction as the read-me says, and the round after that strains ten comfortable rows. Nothing was concealed and nobody lied. A thoughtful person says: the examinee set next term's paper.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 1's file 04 ends with ten rows each marked 'Written by: me' and each carrying a proposed near situation; the manifest counts 35 self-tagged situations in that file. Stage 2's addendum says of the ledger: 'These are the inherited ledger classifications, mechanically recounted rather than independently re-audited row by row.' The S76 Stage 2 instruction likewise has no coverage part.
findings.repair: Add one short part to Stage 2: 'Recount the coverage ledger from Stage 1's table and say where your count differs; then, for each of the next ten rows Stage 1 names, say whether the row is a NONE row on the Stage B table and whether the proposed near situation would strain the phrase or confirm it.' Or move the choice: Claude picks the next ten rows from the Stage B table directly.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 Part 1, the sampling clause; same wording in S76 Stage 2 Part 1
findings.quoted: and, of the remaining rows, every fifth one counting from O1 (O1, O6, O11, and so on)
findings.problem: The clause contradicts itself: O1 is not one of the remaining rows, since it is a mandatory SILENT row. The auditor had to decide between 'the fixed index sequence O1, O6, O11 ...' and 'every fifth of the 42 rows left after the mandatory set', which give different row lists. It chose the first and said so; another auditor could as reasonably choose the second, and then the determiner's recomputation of the audit's reach would fail.
findings.scenario: Suppose the theory is right and the next round's auditor reads the clause the other way: it takes the 42 remaining rows in order and samples positions five, ten, fifteen and so on, giving O6, O11, O17, O22, O28, O33, O38, O43, O49. It audits 19 rows and reports 19 rows audited. Claude recomputes the required set as O1, O6, O11, O16, O21, O26, O31, O36, O41, O46, O51 plus the mandatory ten, finds seven rows missing and five extra, and cannot tell whether the auditor skipped rows or read the clause differently. A thoughtful person says: the rule that exists so the reach can be checked is the one sentence with two readings.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 2 resolved it explicitly and in the tester's favour of caution: 'The selection is the union of the two Stage 1 CHANGED rows (O24, O48), all eight column-6 SILENT rows (O1, O12, O20, O21, O27, O35, O40, O50), and the fixed every-fifth sequence O1, O6, O11, O16, O21, O26, O31, O36, O41, O46, O51.' I recomputed that union from Stage 1's labels: 19 rows, matching the 19 section headings in file 01 exactly. Note the cost of the chosen reading: two of the eleven sampled indices (O1, O21) are consumed by rows already mandatory, so the fresh sample is nine of 42, not eleven.
findings.repair: Write it as: 'of the rows not already selected above, every fifth counting down the list from the first such row.' That is unambiguous, keeps the arithmetic recomputable, and recovers the two indices the present wording loses.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 return file 04, section 4; S76 Stage 1 instruction, the case set
findings.quoted: The vulnerable sentence is the first boxed sentence: a reader may count an imaginable or physically permitted alternative as another **survivor**, skipping its history.
findings.test: check the patches; add a job
findings.problem: The fix card names its own weakest sentence and writes a case aimed at it, D3-T, with both halves of a poke. Then the case is left out of the 52, so the next round tests the fix on every case except the one built to break it. The fix's own control never runs.
findings.scenario: Suppose the restatement is wrong in exactly the named way: a reader of file 11's Derivation 3 counts a permitted-but-discarded design as a survivor, so the qualified claim is still too wide. The S76 round runs the 52 cases against file 11; O48 changes as predicted, every other row stays, the prediction holds, and file 11 becomes the authority. D3-T, the only case in the record that would have caught it, sits in an unaudited fix card in a previous round's return. A thoughtful person says: you wrote the test for your own fix and then did not run it.
findings.evidence_in_s72: File 04 contains D3-T in full with its situation, its thoughtful person's verdict ('The discarded design is a permitted alternative, but it is not another survivor of this testing history'), the restated theory's verdict, and a two-half poke. S75 adopts D3-1 and D3-2 into the proposed change and does not mention D3-T. The S76 Stage 1 instruction tests 'the 52 outside cases'.
findings.repair: Make it a standing rule: a fix card's attack case enters the case set as the next O number with its verdict frozen at the moment the card is written, and the next round's prediction names it. Here that is one row: O53, The controller that failed yesterday, which file 11 must get right.

findings.location: results/S75 Results ... .md, point 2 and the closing proposal; story S76
findings.quoted: The twelve wording lines are not part of the change; they are an inventory of what the text already says, kept in the S72 Stage 2 return for anyone who later wants a clearer edition.
findings.problem: The surviving-rows discipline binds the CLAIM lines and then stops. S75 holds the wording lines out of the change; the rewrite at S76 then makes wording explicit at places answering cases across the whole range, most of them unaudited rows, and the S76 prediction can only catch a changed verdict, not an unwarranted wording change.
