Stage 2's Part 1 dispute is exactly that reasoning, and its file 04 then uses O24 as "positive control", the role Part 4 named. Take the split away and ask what the single-stage S71 would have produced: S71's own Part 3 already said "two cases it must leave alone (O24 and one more)", so one agent reading the same brief had the same cue. The split's demonstrated yield in this round is one card-placement correction (O52) that nothing in the brief pre-assigned.
findings.scenario: Suppose Stage 1 had labelled a third row CHANGED that the instruction had not mentioned. Nothing in Part 4 pre-assigns that row a control role, and nothing else in Stage 2's brief requires it to survive, so its fate would rest on Stage 2's own reading — untested here, because it never happened. On the one row where the brief did speak, the auditor's finding matched the brief. A thoughtful person says: you cannot show a second reader is catching things by pointing at the thing you told him to expect.
findings.evidence_in_s72: results/S72 Stage 2 audit - return/04, section 2 is headed "O24 — positive control at one specified unseen setting" and closes "its role is preservation, not a second changed-case warrant" — the disposition Part 4 named. The unprompted correction is in file 02: "**DISAGREE with Stage 1's PLACED-on-the-original-pair mark.**"
findings.repair: Write Part 4 without naming the controls: "two cases the restatement must leave alone, which you choose and justify." Then a control that survives is the auditor's judgement, and a disputed label is the split's own catch. Report the split's yield each round as the list of corrections it made that the instruction did not foreshadow.

findings.location: The whole pattern; records/Semantics - Lessons.md, lesson 26; HV Skill references/testing-against-cases.md §3
findings.quoted: Lesson 26: "run any test you write on the thing it is meant to catch and on its nearest innocent neighbour." Story S75: "The two-stage form worked on its first use".
findings.test: run the test on what it should catch and its innocent neighbour; flip
findings.problem: The pattern has been run once, on a theory the record describes as having survived every round so far, and pronounced working. It has never been run on a theory known to be wrong, and no prediction was written down beforehand saying what a failing run would look like. The project's own lesson 26 requires exactly that of any test it writes, and the pattern is a test it wrote. Without it, "the two-stage form worked" is supported by one run that found the finding it was told to find.
findings.scenario: Take file 10, plant two errors: one in a Part that four cards touch (say Part XI's production predicate, touched by O13, O20, O25, O26), and one in a Part no card touches (Part VIII's bound). Run the S72 Stage 1 and Stage 2 packs unchanged. If Stage 1's column 6 stays at zero disagreements, the pattern cannot fail a wrong theory even where cases exist; if it catches the first and misses the second, the reach is exactly the case set and the write-up must say so. As it stands, nobody knows which of those three outcomes would happen. A thoughtful person says: a clean sweep on cases you wrote is a reason to attack, not a result.
findings.evidence_in_s72: none seen — no seeded-error run appears anywhere in tests/, results/ or the story, and story S75's verdict on the form is drawn from the same round it is judging.
findings.repair: Run the seeded-error trial described above before file 11 is made the authority, with the two planted errors written down and sealed first. Record what each stage returned against the sealed list. That single run turns "the two-stage form worked" from an assertion into a result.

findings.location: tests/S76 Stage 1 testing…md, "Predictions, fixed before the run" and Part 1 column 3; tests/Instruction pack - build.py, the EXTRA map and the S75 copy
findings.quoted: "**Predictions, fixed before the run.** O48 (the forbidden wire) changes from file 10's verdict to the thoughtful person's. Every other case keeps the verdict file 10 gave. Any other change is a finding against the rewrite, whichever way it goes." Column 3: "The verdict under file 10, bare, as the S72 Stage 1 table gave it in its column 3, quoted."
findings.problem: Freezing the prediction is the right move and is the pattern's best part; handing it to the agent whose output it is meant to constrain is not. The S76 Stage 1 pack also carries Claude's determination (build.py copies S75 into `returns/`) and both S72 returns, so the tester reads the conclusion, the prediction and the previous table before it fills a row. And its column 3 is not re-derived: it copies the S72 Stage 1 verdicts, thirty-three of which no auditor has opened. The comparison the new round makes is therefore between file 11 and an unaudited transcript of file 10.
findings.scenario: Suppose file 11's rewrite silently changed a verdict on O43, an unaudited row. The S76 tester, holding the prediction "Every other case keeps the verdict file 10 gave" and the S72 text of file 10's verdict in column 3, writes a reading of file 11 that matches the copied column 3 and marks SAME. Stage 2 audits every CHANGED, every SILENT and every fifth, and O43 falls outside. The prediction holds; file 11 becomes the authority. A thoughtful person says: a prediction handed to the person producing the evidence, checked against a copied baseline, is a target, not a test.
findings.evidence_in_s72: none seen for the outcome — round S76 has not returned. The construction is visible in build.py: `EXTRA = {… "S76-1": ["S72 Stage 1 testing - return", "S72 Stage 2 audit - return"]}` and `put(… "S75 Results …", "returns/S75 Results - the bare version test, audited.md")` for every S76 pack.
findings.repair: Keep the prediction and S75 out of Stage 1's pack; put them in Stage 2's, so the auditor can score the tester against a prediction the tester never saw. Have Stage 1 re-derive file 10's bare verdict for any row where it marks CHANGED, instead of quoting the S72 table, and flag every copied row as unaudited.

findings.location: tests/Instruction pack - read me first for the agent.md, "Who is who"; records/Semantics - project story.md throughout
findings.quoted: Read-me: "**You** are 'the other model' in every file here. Earlier rounds were run by earlier agents in the same role". Story S72: "run by separate agents, with Claude reading both returns and determining the results".
findings.problem: "A second agent" is a fresh context, not a different reader. The record never names which model ran either stage — I searched records/ and tests/ and found only "another model". Two runs of the same model on the same pack share their blind spots, so agreement between the stages is weaker evidence than it looks; the split buys independence from memory, which the owner fixed at decision S5, and not independence of judgement, which is what an audit is for.
findings.scenario: Suppose the model reads file 10's Part XI production predicate the same wrong way every time it is asked. Stage 1 writes that reading into six rows. Stage 2, a fresh context of the same model, re-derives the same reading from the same text and writes AGREE on each. The counts show nineteen agreements, the determination treats them as two readings that met, and the shared error passes through into file 11. A thoughtful person says: the same scale twice is one weighing.
findings.evidence_in_s72: none seen either way — the model behind each return is not recorded, so this cannot be settled from the files. The agreement pattern (19 of 19 on both verdict columns, with the only substantive dispute on a mark rather than a reading) is consistent with both a careful check and a correlated one.
findings.repair: Record the model and version that ran each stage in the manifest, and run Stage 2 on a different model family from Stage 1 for one round. If the DISAGREE count on the sampled rows moves, the split's independence was resting on the reader and not on the fresh context.

harder_to_vary: Cut the answer out of the packs and make the deliverables conditional. Stage 1's framing says which comparison to run and never which rows will move; Stage 2's Part 4 reads "for each row your Part 1 confirms CHANGED, fill one fix card; if none survives, say so and write no card," with the controls chosen by the auditor rather than named in the brief. Keep Claude's prior reading (the S71 paragraph, the S76 prediction) sealed and compare it with the return afterwards. Then a round that finds nothing is a possible outcome, which it currently is not.

Make one sample blind on both sides. Add a fourth audit trigger that does not read Stage 1: a fixed sample of rows Stage 1 marked SAME and agreeing, handed to Stage 2 with columns 3, 4 and 5 blanked, filled from the theory and the card alone, and only then compared. And commission a held-out block of cases from an author who has not read file 10, verdicts sealed until the return is in, mixed into the table so that neither agent can tell which rows are held out. Until one such block exists, the zero disagreements in all 52 rows say nothing about the theory.

Run the pattern on what it is meant to catch and on its innocent neighbour, and write the prediction first. Take file 10, plant one error in a Part four cards touch and one in a Part no card touches, seal the list, run both packs unchanged, and record what each stage returned. The same run answers three questions at once: can Stage 1's column 6 ever fire, does the fixed every-fifth sample reach an unflagged error, and is the pattern's reach exactly the case set.
independence.next_step: Before file 11 is made the authority, run the seeded-error trial: copy file 10, plant one error in Part XI (four cards touch it) and one in Part VIII's accumulated-error bound (no card touches it), seal the two-line list, send the unchanged S72 Stage 1 and Stage 2 packs against the doctored file, and write down which of the two each stage reported. That single round settles whether the pattern can fail a wrong theory, and where its reach stops.
independence.not_shown: This does not show that file 10 or file 11 is false, nor that the Derivation 3 finding is wrong — I verified the proof sentence and the population definition against file 10 by hand (lines 569–573 and 210) and the gap between the claim's \"there exists a transport t'\" and Part IV's population is real. It does not show the two agents worked carelessly: both returns are unusually disciplined, both name their own limits in writing, and Stage 2's scope note volunteers the anchoring problem that is my fourth finding. It does not settle whether the two stages were run by the same model, because the record never says. It does not touch the owner's fixed choices (push to main, a fresh agent per step, returns held unchanged, zips, positive wording), and I have spent no finding on them. I read the two S72 return folders' MANIFEST, PARKED, Stage 1 files 01 and 02, and Stage 2 files 01, 02 (outline and the O52 and clause-table sections), 03 (counts and verdict-bearing section), 04 and 05 in full, and sampled Stage 1 files 03, 04 and 05 rather than reading them through; a defect sitting only in Stage 1's coverage file or in the unquoted body of its quotations register would not have reached me. Round S76 has not returned, so everything I say about it is about its instructions and its pack, not its result. And hard to vary is not true: a pattern that passes every test here could still be finding the wrong things.

overall.summary: The two-stage pattern does several things it says it does, and does them well: the identifier on every verdict lets a stranger check a row (all 119 resolved, none absent); the quotation check against file 10 is real, and I confirmed three of its entries by hand at lines 569–573, 210 and 38; the AGREE/DISAGREE and CONFIRMED/DISPUTED marks can fire and did, on O24's label and O52's placement; the "Held back by the audit" list has a gauge and was used; the judgement-phrase gauge is reported at start and end. Where it fails is independence, and it fails in the same place at every link. Claude wrote the theory's revisions, wrote O15 to O52 with the thoughtful person's verdict fixed first, wrote both stage instructions, decides what goes in each pack, reads both returns, and determines the result — and both instructions name the round's answer in their second paragraph ("O24 and O48 against Derivation 3"), while Stage 2's Part 4 pre-titles the fix card, names O48 as the forcing case and assigns O24 the control role that Stage 2 then gives it. Stage 2 is handed Stage 1's whole return and says in writing that its "expectation" was not blind; it returned 19 AGREE and 0 DISAGREE on both verdict columns. Three of the four audit triggers are computed from Stage 1's own output, so Stage 1's misses are reachable only by a fixed one-in-five sample, and the 33 unaudited rows are carried forward verbatim as S76's baseline for file 10. The bare theory disagrees with the thoughtful person on nought of 52 cases — which, against verdicts written by the theory's own reviser and forbidden to be questioned, is the skill's "passing your own test" in plain sight. The reach is exactly the case set: R2 J's second qualification, the missing initial-error term in Part VIII, is quoted verbatim in every citation both agents used, was named unresolved by Stage 2, is absent from S75, and file 11 carries file 10's sentence unchanged at line 361. The repairs are small and specific: take the answer out of the packs, make the deliverables conditional, blind one sample on both sides, and run the pattern once on a theory known to be wrong.

independence.question_frozen: Whether the two-stage testing-then-audit pattern makes sense as a way of finding what is wrong with Claude Fable Semantics, over the rounds run so far (S72 in full, S76 as set up) and over the theory as it stands in files 10 and 11. Three things are asked and all three answered: (1) internally, does each part do what its instruction says, as the S72 returns show; (2) as a test, can the pattern fail a wrong theory and pass a right one, and is there a route by which a wrong theory gets reported as wrong rather than absorbed by a reading, a PARKED file or a held-back list; (3) as an explanation of why this method finds what is wrong with the theory, is each part held in place by a job, and does swapping a part for its neighbour break something. My lens is independence: where in the chain from theory-author to determination can the pattern agree with its author by construction. The question is held still: I am not asking whether the theory is true, nor whether the agents did careful work, nor whether the owner's fixed choices are good ones.

whole_checks.catch_alls: Four catch-alls, three with working gauges. PARKED: gauge is one printed line per idea; both returns read "PARKED LIST EMPTY", which is either an honest zero or lesson 35's trap, and nothing in the returns tells them apart. "Held back by the audit": gauge is the list with a reason per line; it fired once, on the S70 CLAIM sentence, and its second row honestly reads "None" for quotation defects — the best-behaved of the four. SILENT: gauge is the eight named rows, carried into S76 Stage 1 as a required check ("for each of the eight cases the S72 round found SILENT under file 10 … one sentence saying whether file 11 now names the declared input") — a real forward gauge. The declared-inputs / open-points / homeless inventory: gauge is the count at both ends of the round, 2-4-1 at start and 2-4-1 at end, which would show a judgement being quietly absorbed. The one catch-all with no gauge is the unaudited remainder: 33 rows pass through on Stage 1's word into S76's column 3, and nothing measures whether they are swallowing anything. "Every fifth row" is the nearest thing to a gauge for it, and nine rows out of forty-two is a thin one.
whole_checks.change_list_gaps: Held fixed every round: the case set (the same 52, plus three per round), the author of every case and every reference verdict (Claude), the rule that no agent may question a verdict, the reading conventions, the pack contents as Claude chooses them, and the model family (never recorded). Varied: which theory file is under test (10, then 11), which amendments are read in, which rows the audit samples, the split into two stages from S72. So the pattern has never been run with a different case set, a different verdict author, a different reference standard, or a known-wrong theory. The three things whose variation would bite hardest are exactly the three never varied.
whole_checks.direction: Backward, on the axis that matters, and forward on two narrower ones. Backward: the result — Derivation 3 needs R2 J's qualification, forced by O48 — was reached by Claude at S71 from the S70 return, written into the second paragraph of both S72 instructions, made the title and content of Stage 2's Part 4, and then returned by both agents and written up by Claude as the round's finding. Poke the supposed cause and the effect moves: change which derivation the framing paragraph names and there is no reason to think the CHANGED list would look the same. Forward: the quotation check runs from file 10's text to a mark and could have come back DIFFERS; the fixed every-fifth sample runs from the card and the theory to a verdict and could have come back DISAGREE. Both came back clean.
whole_checks.flip: Had file 10 been badly wrong in a way its author did not anticipate, the same two-stage run would not have reported it. The route by which a wrong theory gets reported is Stage 1's column 6 — "Where column 3 disagrees with column 2, one sentence: what in the bare earlier version gives the wrong verdict, quoted" — and that branch has never fired in 52 rows; every entry reads "No disagreement" or SILENT. The audit then selects on CHANGED, SILENT and disagreement, so a wrong verdict that Stage 1 wrote up as agreement is reachable only by the one-in-five fixed sample. A failing run would have looked different in one visible way: column 6 would carry a quoted sentence of file 10 and the row would be pulled into the audit by the third trigger. That has not happened once. The concrete case is already on the record: R2 J's Part VIII initial-error qualification is quoted verbatim in every T-R27 citation both agents used, Stage 2 names it unresolved, no card exercises Part VIII, and file 11 carries file 10's bound unchanged at line 361 — a place where the theory may be wrong, which the pattern reported nowhere because nobody wrote a card for it.
whole_checks.hidden_answer: Yes, in four places, each checkable. In the instructions: "The S70 addendum's heading (11) found one place where it does (O24 and O48 against Derivation 3). This stage finds every such place" — in both stages' packs. In Stage 2's Part 4: the card's title names Derivation 3, its field 1 names O48, its field 2 names O24 as a case to leave alone. In the case set: every card from O15 on was written by Claude against a named amendment or Stage B row, with the thoughtful person's verdict fixed first, and O48's verdict is phrased in R2 J's own vocabulary ("The premise is not met"). And in the reference standard itself: several cases are the hard-to-vary skill's worked examples, and file 10's Part 0 attack (A) already names "lookup tables, reversed calculations, conclusion-as-premise" — which are O2, O4 and O37 — as things the theory handles.
whole_checks.jobs_origin: Given by the owner (one job, in his words at S7): split into two stages, testing and audit, with Claude reading both and determining results. Fixed by the owner and not tested here: a fresh agent per step (S5), returns held unchanged and zips (S5), push to main and edit only inside the project (S6), positive wording (decision 20). Everything else is Claude's, and so is added: that the round should find what is wrong with the theory; that the synthesis be built only from surviving rows; that every verdict carry an identifier; that the audit sample be CHANGED plus SILENT plus disagreeing plus every fifth; that the quotations file stand alone; that draft lines resting on disputed rows be held back; that the prediction be frozen. A part held only by a job Claude added is held if that job is real — and the largest of them, "find what is wrong with the theory", is the one the case set's authorship puts in doubt.
whole_checks.parts_origin: Fitted: the case set, grown one batch per round, each batch aimed at the rows or amendments the previous round left open — so it is held in place exactly where it has been tested and says nothing about Parts no card has reached (Part VIII is the live example). The audit sampling rule, fitted to the shape of Stage 1's output. The judgement-phrase gauge, fitted after lesson 35 showed the earlier pass was too easy. Built: the identifier on every verdict, worked out from the fresh-agent requirement and stating its own reason inside the instruction, which is why it is the hardest part here to vary. The self-standing quotations file, same. The "Held back by the audit" list, built from the S70 round's problem of unevidenced draft lines. Asserted: the two-stage split (the owner said so); the thoughtful person's verdicts (written down and made unquestionable by instruction); "an outside author" as a name for the case author.
whole_checks.pulls: Four pairs pull. (1) Fresh agent with no memory against a pack that must carry every earlier round: independence gives way, because the pack carries the earlier rounds and the earlier rounds carry the answer; what would show the line is in the wrong place is a pack holding only the theory, the cards and the instruction producing the same CHANGED list. (2) An audit that must check Stage 1 against an audit that must not be anchored by it: anchoring gives way — Stage 2 says so itself; the line could be drawn at "the sampled rows come with Stage 1's columns blanked until you have written your own". (3) Positive wording against exactness: the instruction cannot say "do not assume the card's verdict", so it says "Keep every situation and every verdict exactly as written", which forbids the one criticism that would catch a bad reference verdict. (4) Audit cost against carrying the result forward: nineteen of fifty-two is affordable, and the thirty-three unaudited rows then become S76's quoted baseline for file 10, so the saving is spent twice.
whole_checks.rivals: Single stage (S71, superseded unsent): tell them apart by what the second reader corrected that the brief did not foreshadow. In S72 that is one item, O52's card placement; the O24 dispute was pre-assigned by Part 4's control, and S71's own Part 3 carried the same cue. Two independent testers with a tiebreak: separated by whether the second set of verdicts was produced without sight of the first; here 19 of 19 agreements on both verdict columns cannot distinguish a check from a recognition. Cases written blind by an outside model with hidden verdicts: separated by whether the theory's nought-wrong-in-fifty-two survives; this is the change that would tell the most apart and has never been made. Audit by a different model family: separated by whether the DISAGREE count moves; unknown, because the record never names the model. A human adjudicator in place of Claude's determination: separated on the one sentence of S75 I found wrong (line 23's attribution of all nineteen agreements to the fixed sample) and on whether the unexercised amendment sentences reach "What this does not show". A pre-registered results template: S76 has the beginnings of one in its frozen prediction, and it is handed to the tester, so it does not yet separate the two.

Stage 2 file 01: "SAME includes a preserved unresolved judgement; CHANGED requires a different material reading of this case." S75: "Stage 2 is right on the instruction's own terms: column 5 asks whether the verdict on the case changes, and it does not."
findings.test: hunt the answer in the starting points
findings.problem: The instruction never says what counts as a change. The rule that decides every one of the 52 rows was written by the agent being graded, in its own preamble, after it had read the cases; Stage 2 inherited it (Stage 1's return is inside Stage 2's pack) and restated it; and the determination then cited it as "the instruction's own terms", which are not its terms. The rule is what produces the headline "one amendment changes one verdict": forty-four rows carry the identical boilerplate "SAME. No change in this case; clarification is not itself a changed verdict."
findings.scenario: Suppose file 10 is wrong in the way O24 is: a dozen theorems each claim more than their proofs give, and each amendment narrows a theorem's reach without flipping the case's own answer. Stage 1 marks the dozen CHANGED. Stage 2, applying the material-verdict rule, disputes all twelve exactly as it disputed O24. The determination reports "no amendment changes any verdict; the twenty wording lines are confirmed as wording", and a rewrite is judged unearned. A thoughtful person says twelve passages of the theory overreach their own proofs, and that is precisely the list a new version should be built from. Now run the same rule on the thing it should catch: O48, where bare file 10 says a differing survivor exists and the qualified reading says none does. The rule separates O48 from O24 correctly. So the rule is not merely convenient; it is defensible. It is still not the rule the instruction stated, and the round was saved only because O48 happened to exist and forced the same repair anyway.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 1 file 01 lines 4-10 state the rule; the phrase "clarification is not itself a changed verdict" appears in 44 of 52 column-5 cells. Stage 2 file 01 restates it before auditing. Stage 2's "Disputed rows" retires O24 with "Columns 3 and 4 accurately describe the respective theoretical readings; the CHANGED label is what fails." S75 point 1 then reports one changed verdict in 52.
findings.repair: Put the test in the instruction, before the run, and split it in two columns: "does the case's own verdict change?" and "does the claim of the passage it rests on change?". A scope narrowing is then reported as a scope narrowing instead of disappearing into SAME. Until that is written, the determination must say in one line that the SAME rule was supplied by the agents, not the instruction.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 instruction, Part 5; S72 Stage 2 return file 05, "Explicit already; every case agreed"; S75 point 2; story S76
findings.quoted: Instruction: "a line whose case shows the same reading under the bare earlier version and the amended one is kept in a second list headed “Explicit already; every case agreed”". S75: "Stage 2's inventory of twelve such lines (W01 to W12) is explicit already in the Parts it names." Story S76: "the twelve wording lines the S72 audit found explicit already are made explicit at their places".
findings.problem: The bin's name asserts a conclusion its membership test does not establish. The test is "bare and amended readings agree on this case"; the name says "the Parts already say this sentence". Two readings can agree because the text says the thing, or because the text says nothing and both readings are silent. The determination repeated the name as a finding, and the rewrite then wrote the sentences into file 11 — which is only needed if they were not explicit already. It is a catch-all with no gauge: nothing printed anywhere would show it swallowing a claim change.
findings.scenario: W08 reads "A protected obligation is assessed with its condition and occasions fixed, and an omitted condition cannot be chosen from the desired no-loss verdict", warranted by "O35; file 01, O35: SAME; Part XI; [T-E16; T-C03]". T-C03 is H65, which Stage 1's own quotations file tags "Version: clause. Part: Not authority text" — a clause an earlier agent wrote at S65 precisely because, as story S70 records, "the protected condition's temporal scope had never been stated" in file 10. I checked the text by hand: file 10 line 438 is "**Repair.** For claimed obligations \(O\) and protected obligations \(P\), fixed for the comparison," and says nothing about occasions; file 11 line 433 adds "each as a stated condition over stated occasions, and a protected condition is lost exactly when it fails on an occasion it covers." So a sentence filed under "Explicit already" was not in the authority, is sourced to a proposed clause, and has now been added to the theory as a new biconditional under a prediction that says nothing but O48 changes. A thoughtful person calls that a claim added without a case forcing it.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 2 file 05 line 159 is honest about the test it ran — "Here “agreed” means the **bare and amended material readings agree with each other**" — and line 176 says "These lines are a presentation/retention inventory" and "The sentences are present-audit formulations, not asserted verbatim authority text." The determination dropped both caveats and kept the bin's name.
findings.repair: Rename the bin to what it measures: "Bare and amended agree on this case". Require any line claiming the authority already says it to carry a verbatim quotation from the authority in its warrant column, with clause identifiers (T-C…) barred from that column. Then count the lines that survive; that count is the bin's gauge.

findings.location: S72 Stage 1 instruction, column 6 and "Keep every situation and every verdict exactly as written"; the whole table; S75 point 4
findings.quoted: Instruction: "Keep every situation and every verdict exactly as written." And: "6. Where column 3 disagrees with column 2, one sentence: what in the bare earlier version gives the wrong verdict, quoted, or that the earlier version is silent on the case (SILENT)."
findings.test: run the test on what it should catch and its innocent neighbour
findings.problem: A failed test knocks down a bundle: the claim, the case's stipulations, the agent's reading of the theory, and the standard the case is scored against. The table has one column for the first of those and no field at all for the other three. Column 6 is worded so that a disagreement can only be the theory's fault. The verdicts against which everything is scored are written by the same session that writes the instruction, the amendments-under-test and the determination, and both agents are forbidden to touch them. The one place where the bundle is properly opened is the fix card's field 6, and it is not required of ordinary rows.
findings.scenario: O48's situation stipulates "every device in the stated population is built without that wire" and its thoughtful verdict says "Then there is no alternative in that population ... The premise is not met." The verdict restates the stipulation. If "population" in the case is not what Part IV's \(\mathcal T\) means, the thing refuted is the case's reading, not Derivation 3, and no column exists in which that could be written. Run the same instrument on its innocent neighbour: a case whose situation and verdict come apart, where the theory really is wrong. The table reports it the same way — column 6, "what in the bare earlier version gives the wrong verdict". The two are indistinguishable in the return's form. What saves O48 is outside the table: the fix card's field 6 answers "Yes, the proof's construction step already assumes that a different admitted relation can yield another eligible survivor, but it neither states that availability as the claim's hypothesis nor establishes the same-population and realizability conditions", which makes the defect internal to file 10 and independent of the case and of R2 — and an outside judge reached it from the text alone (log S73).
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 2 file 04, field 6, quotes file 10's proof sentence "Alter \(L_{j}(a,b)\) for one \((a,b)\notin H\) to any other admitted relation" and gives the one-sentence answer above. I confirmed the quotation by hand against file 10 lines 569-573. No row of the table has a field for the case or the standard failing; the workflow the pack calls the audit skill does have one ("Best reply on the theory's behalf: / Does the difference survive the reply:") and the two-stage table drops it.
findings.repair: Add one required line to every CHANGED row and every row where column 3 disagrees with column 2: which of the four failed — the claim, the case's stipulation, the reading of the theory, or the thoughtful person's verdict — and why not the other three. Restore the workflow's "best reply on the theory's behalf" as a column, so the strongest defence is on the record before a row is counted as a defect.

findings.location: S76 Stage 1 instruction, Part 1, column 3; S75 "What this does not show"

findings.location: authority/11, Part XIV "Declared inputs" (line 514) and Part XI (line 433); story S76; S72 Stage 2 return file 05, heading (4)
findings.quoted: File 11: "**Declared inputs.** Besides the two primitives, some claims take stated inputs that the semantics records and does not supply ... A verdict that depends on one of these is a verdict given the input; where the input is missing, the verdict is unsettled and the semantics says so rather than choosing the input from the verdict wanted." Story S76: "a “Declared inputs” paragraph in Part XIV names the obligations and their occasions, the scope of a contract, and the system boundary and continuity, as inputs the semantics records and does not supply, so the gauge's seven rows have a stated home."
findings.problem: SILENT is the pattern's catch-all and it currently has a good gauge: the count of live borrowed rows, printed at the start and end of the audit, and the rule that every SILENT row is audited in full. File 11 converts each of those eight silences from an unexplained gap into a stated feature of the theory. That may be the right move, but it disarms the gauge: under file 11 a SILENT row is what the theory promises, so the count can never rise, and the S76 test cannot tell a theory that explains its silences from one that has been given a licence to be silent. A patch that absorbs the failures it was written for and nothing else is the classic easy-to-vary repair, and here it arrives under a prediction that says nothing changes.
findings.scenario: Stage 1 of S76 reaches O35. File 11 now says the obligations are declared inputs with their occasions, and that a missing input leaves the verdict unsettled. The agent writes SILENT, marks SAME against S72's SILENT, and under the instruction's own bullet — "for each of the eight cases the S72 round found SILENT under file 10 ... one sentence saying whether file 11 now names the declared input the case lacks" — answers yes. All eight come out the same way. The prediction holds; the gauge reads seven; and a thoughtful person asks what reading of file 11 would ever make the gauge read eight.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 2 file 05, heading (4), prints the gauge as a table: "Stage 1 inherited position at audit start | 2 | 4 | 1 | 7" and "Stage 2 end | 2 | 4 | 1 | 7", with the note "Correcting a coverage label or qualifying Derivation 3 does not remove a separate value, grounding, scope or comparative judgement." That is the gauge working under file 10.
findings.repair: Give the catch-all a gauge that still reads under file 11. For each SILENT row require two lines: the exact input file 11 says is missing, and the smallest addition to the case that would make file 11 give a verdict. A SILENT row where the agent cannot name the missing input, or cannot name an addition that would settle it, counts against the rewrite. Record the gauge reading round by round beside the seven.

findings.location: Decision S7; S75 "What the two agents found, and where they differed" and "The determination"

The determination's form is a paragraph per disagreement giving a reason; a reader cannot see whether the reason was reached from file 10 or from Stage 2's argument. findings.location: S72 Stage 2 instruction, Part 1, sampling clause
findings.quoted: "and, of the remaining rows, every fifth one counting from O1 (O1, O6, O11, and so on)"
findings.problem: The clause contradicts its own example. "Of the remaining rows" means after the CHANGED, SILENT and disagreeing rows are removed; the example counts O1, which is itself one of the eight SILENT rows and therefore not remaining. Two rounds' coverage figures then mean different things and cannot be added or compared, and neither return says which reading it took — except that this one did, which is why the ambiguity is visible at all.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 2 file 01: "The selection is the union of ... and the fixed every-fifth sequence O1, O6, O11, O16, O21, O26, O31, O36, O41, O46, O51 ... The union is **19 rows**". O1 and O21 are in the union twice.

findings.location: S72 Stage 2 instruction, Part 3; S72 Stage 2 return file 03, "Method and scope"; S75 "What this does not show"
findings.quoted: Instruction: "For every R2 sentence, find it in the returns in this pack and mark it likewise." Stage 2: "For an R2 entry, the comparison is against the prior S62/S64 return that Stage 1 cites, not against Stage 1's own repetition."
findings.problem: The verbatim check has three links and verifies two of them. R2 has never been in the repository, so "VERBATIM" for an R2 sentence means "identical to an earlier agent's quotation of a file nobody here has seen". A misquotation made at S62 or S64 is indistinguishable from the real sentence and would be marked VERBATIM by every later round.
findings.scenario: The S64 agent paraphrased J's Part XVI.3 sentence when it built its quotations file. Every round since, including both S72 stages, checks against that paraphrase and finds it verbatim. The determination reports "the quotation is verbatim", and file 11 is rewritten around an amendment nobody wrote. A thoughtful person says the chain was never anchored. What saves this particular case is that the finding does not need R2 at all: the fix card shows file 10's own proof already assumes what its claim omits, and that quotation was checked against file 10 itself.
findings.evidence_in_s72: Stage 2 file 03 reports 119 of 119 verbatim and names the locators, which for R2 entries are `returns/S62 Stage D and report - return/07 Quotations.md` and `returns/S64 Near cases - return/05 Quotations.md`, never an R2 file. S75 declares the limit: "R2 was read from the sentences the returns quote; the full R2 file has never been in the repository."
findings.repair: Mark R2 entries with a third status, CHAINED, rather than VERBATIM, and print in the manifest how many load-bearing verdicts rest on a chained quotation. Until the R2 file is supplied, require any CLAIM line resting on a chained sentence to carry a second, independent warrant from the authority itself — which the Derivation 3 line already has.

harder_to_vary: Run Stage 1 twice, by two fresh agents, on the same pack, and print the rows where the two tables differ. The method currently has no measure of how much of a verdict is the theory and how much is the reader, and it is the cheapest job to add because the pattern already spawns fresh agents. If two independent testers disagree on ten of fifty-two rows, the table is mostly measuring the reader and every count in S75 changes meaning. If they disagree on none, the audit's nineteen-for-nineteen agreement stops being ambiguous and starts being evidence.

Fix the reading rules in the instruction instead of letting the graded agent supply them. Write the SAME/CHANGED test in two columns (does the case's verdict change; does the passage's claim change), rename "Explicit already; every case agreed" to "Bare and amended agree on this case", and bar clause identifiers from the warrant column of any line claiming the authority already says something. Each of these three is one sentence in the instruction and each one closes a route by which a real change is absorbed by a name.

Strip the answer out of the tested agent's pack: drop S75 and the S72 Stage 2 return from the S76-1 pack, move the prediction below build.py's owner-section marker, and have Claude choose the audit's residual sample after the Stage 1 return arrives. The prediction stays frozen and written down; it is simply held by the adjudicator instead of handed to the instrument, which is the whole difference between a pre-registration and a target.
determination.next_step: Before the S76 packs go out, make three edits to build.py and the two S76 instructions: remove `S75` and `S72 Stage 2 audit - return` from the S76-1 pack, move the \"Predictions, fixed before the run\" paragraph below the `\\n---\\n(Below this line` marker that build.py already strips, and add to S76 Stage 1's column 5 the two-part SAME/CHANGED test (case verdict, passage claim) with a worked example of each. Then send Stage 1.
determination.not_shown: This is a reading of the pattern, not of the theory: nothing here bears on whether file 10 or file 11 is true, and nothing here shows the Derivation 3 finding is wrong — I checked that quotation by hand against file 10 lines 569-573 and the fix card's reasoning is internal to file 10 and survives without R2. I did not audit the thirty-three rows Stage 2 left alone, so I cannot say whether Stage 1 read file 10 correctly there; my findings are about the fact that nobody can, not about what is in them. I did not read the S62, S64, S65 or S70 returns, so the case set's history before O50 is taken from the story entries. I read Stage 1 files 01 and 05 and Stage 2 files 01, 03 (method and table only), 04 and 05 in full, and sampled 02 and Stage 1's 02, 03 and 04. The S76 round has not been run, so every finding about it is about what its packs and instructions make possible, not about what happened; where I say \"none seen\" that is what it means. I did not test the owner's standing choices (push to main, fresh agent per step, returns held unchanged, zips), which are fixed. I did not compare file 10 and file 11 line by line — that is the S76 Stage 1 Part 2 job — beyond the one paragraph on protected obligations that W08 turns on.

overall.summary: The split does a real job and did it. Remove the second stage and the S72 round ships a draft list with two changed verdicts instead of one and a case card placed on the wrong pair; the audit caught both, and a fix card that runs its restatement on the case that forced it, on two cases it must leave alone, and on a self-written attack is the best piece of work in either return. So the pattern passes the first test: it can move a result, and the movement was recorded. Where it is loose is around the split, not in it. The rule that decides SAME from CHANGED on all fifty-two rows was written by the agent being graded, after the data, and the determination adopted it as the instruction's own terms, which it is not; forty-four rows carry the same boilerplate sentence. The bin named "Explicit already; every case agreed" tests only that two readings agree, and one of its twelve lines is demonstrably not explicit in file 10 — file 11 has just added it. The audit's reach is set by the labels of the return it audits, and from S76 the sampling rule and the expected answer both sit inside the tested agent's own pack, so the next round as packed runs backward from the result. Thirty-three unchecked rows become that round's baseline and agreement with them is its pass condition. None of this makes the O48 finding wrong — it is internal to file 10, it was reached again by an outside judge from the text alone, and I checked its quotation by hand — but the round was saved by that case existing, not by the pattern's design. The repairs are small and mostly editorial: put the reading rules in the instruction, take the answer out of the pack, and let the determiner pick the sample after the return arrives.

determination.question_frozen: Does the two-stage pattern — one fresh agent reads the theory bare against all 52 cases with an identifier on every verdict, a second fresh agent checks that return row by row against the sources and builds the fix card and draft list from what survives, and Claude reads both and determines — find what is wrong with Claude Fable Semantics? Over the range of rounds it is meant to run (S72 against file 10, S76 against file 11, and rounds after), and over the range of theories it is meant to handle (a formal semantics of roughly eight to ten thousand words, revised between rounds, tested against a fixed case set that grows by a handful each round). Three things are asked, and I answer all three: whether each part does inside the run what the instruction says it does and the S72 returns show it; whether the pattern can fail a wrong theory and pass a right one, with a route by which a wrong theory is reported wrong rather than absorbed by a reading, a PARKED file or a held-back list; and whether each part is held in place by a job, so that swapping a part for its nearest neighbour breaks something. This is a \"does it achieve its purpose?\" question about a method, not a question about whether the theory is true.

whole_checks.catch_alls: Five, of uneven quality. PARKED: gauge is that it is printed and read; it reads "PARKED LIST EMPTY." in both S72 returns, so it is swallowing nothing, but its stated scope is "procedures, graphs, algorithms, data structures and scoring schemes" and a doubt about a case or about the method has no home anywhere. SILENT: gauge is the live-judgement-rows table, printed at audit start and end (7 and 7), plus the rule that every SILENT row is audited in full — the best-gauged catch-all in the method, and the one file 11's "Declared inputs" paragraph is about to disarm. "Held back by the audit": gauge is that it prints its entries with reasons and prints a null row for the empty category; it held the retirement of S70's O24 line. REVISED ONLY: gauge is a row count (9 rows), declared in the coverage file. "Explicit already; every case agreed": no gauge at all — nothing printed anywhere would show it swallowing a claim change, and W08 shows it doing so. Declared inputs, new in file 11: no gauge yet.
whole_checks.change_list_gaps: The same 52 cases every round, in the same numbering, written by one author with the verdict fixed first. The same author for the instruction, the prediction, the theory, the revision and the determination. The same reading conventions, inherited through the pack rather than re-derived or fixed in writing. The same model family for both stages, so a blind spot the model has is a blind spot both stages have. The first 32 Stage B rows have never been recovered (coverage stays at 80 of 112). R2 has never been in the repository. And the change list never varies the one thing that would tell the reader from the theory: nobody has run Stage 1 twice.
whole_checks.direction: S72 ran forward: the round was set up to find every place an amendment moves a verdict, it found one, and it was not the answer the project expected — S70 had recorded two (O24 and O48) and O24 fell. That is the mark of a test rather than a confirmation. S76 as packed runs backward: the prediction names the answer, the instruction states it, S75 states it twice more, and all three are inside the testing agent's pack before it reads a case.
whole_checks.flip: Partly. The route by which a wrong theory is reported wrong is column 6 — "Where column 3 disagrees with column 2 ... what in the bare earlier version gives the wrong verdict, quoted" — and it was used, once, on O48, and the audit confirmed it and built a restatement from it. So the route is real and exercised. But it is narrow. Column 5, where the round's headline comes from, can only report defects that an amendment happens to fix; a defect nobody drafted an amendment for has no column of its own. Had file 10 been badly wrong in a place R2 never touched, the return would look exactly as it does except for one or two more column-6 sentences, and 34 of the 43 rows where Stage 1 wrote "No disagreement" were never re-read by anyone. Had the theory been badly wrong in the way O24 is — claims wider than their proofs, on a dozen passages — the agents' own SAME rule would have marked all twelve unchanged.
whole_checks.hidden_answer: In three of the four inputs. The cases and the thoughtful person's verdicts are Claude's, written with the verdict fixed first, and O48's verdict ("Then there is no alternative in that population") is close to a restatement of its own stipulation. The prediction is Claude's and is handed to the agent. The reading rule that decides SAME from CHANGED is the graded agent's, written after the data. The one input that is genuinely outside is the convergence at log S73, where an unsolicited judge from another chat reached the Derivation 3 defect from file 10's text alone, with no cases — and that is outside the pattern, not produced by it. What keeps the headline finding honest is that it does not need any of the loaded inputs: the fix card's field 6 shows file 10's own proof sentence assumes what its claim omits, and that quotation was checked against file 10 and by me by hand.
whole_checks.jobs_origin: Given by the owner: the split into testing and audit, and Claude reading both and determining (decision S7, quoted verbatim in the record); an audit by another model under a bounded, positively worded workflow (decision 20). Fixed and not tested here: fresh agent per step, zips, returns held unchanged, push to main (decisions S5, S6). Added by Claude over the rounds and therefore not held by the owner's word: the sampling rule, the identifier-per-verdict rule, the frozen prediction, the three draft lists and their names, the case set and its verdicts, the gauge. Added by me for this reading: that the cases should be outside the project and not only outside the tested agent; that the pattern should measure how much of a verdict is the reader; that the determination should print its own worked reading when the two agents differ. Parts held only by my added jobs are marked "held if" above.
whole_checks.parts_origin: Mostly fitted, round by round, on what the previous round threw up: the split itself came from S71's failure to have anyone check the table; the sampling rule grew out of S62-S70 practice; the three draft lists were written after S70's heading (11) produced a mixed list. Fitted parts are held exactly where they were tested and say nothing about what they have not met — which is why the S76 pack composition, a change none of them was fitted on, broke the blinding without anyone noticing. Built, in the skill's sense: the fix card's six fields with a forcing case, two cases it must leave alone and a self-written attack on its own weakest sentence; that is worked out from the idea and can be caught out. Asserted: the SAME/CHANGED rule and the name "Explicit already; every case agreed" — both simply written down, both load-bearing, neither tested.
whole_checks.pulls: Five pairs, each with a line and a way to see it drawn wrong. Fresh agent with no memory against a pack that must carry every earlier round: the pack grows, and at S76 it now carries the answer; the line is drawn wrong when a file that helps the agent understand the task also tells it the result. Stage 2 must audit Stage 1 row by row against Stage 2 must read independently: row-level precision against anchoring, and Stage 2 said where it gives — it sees Stage 1's answer first. Positive wording (decision 20) against exactness: the positively named bins work for "Held back by the audit" and fail for "Explicit already; every case agreed", where the positive name asserts a conclusion; the line is drawn wrong when a bin's name states a finding its membership test cannot support. Audit reach against cost: 19 of 52, and the 33 become the next round's baseline; the line is drawn wrong when unaudited rows are quoted as established. "Keep every verdict exactly as written" against the ability to report a bad case: repeatability against falsifiability of the standard; the line is drawn wrong when no field exists in which a case, rather than the theory, can fail.
whole_checks.rivals: Single stage (S71): told apart by O24 and O52, which S71 would have shipped. The split wins, and this is the one rival the record decides. Two independent testers with a tiebreak: the strongest rival, costs the same two agents, and nothing on the current change list tells it from the two-stage pattern except the one thing the pattern cannot report — how much of a verdict is the reader rather than the theory. At this level the two are the same explanation of why the method finds what is wrong, and the pattern owes the finer question. Cases written blind by an outside model with hidden verdicts: told apart by whether a clean sweep means anything; on the S72 evidence (44 of 52 agreements on home cases) the pattern cannot tell itself from this rival, which is the honest report. Audit by a different model family: told apart on shared blind spots; never tried, and cheap. A human adjudicator in place of Claude: nothing on the change list separates them, since the determination's only recorded acts are reading two returns and giving reasons; say so rather than claim an advantage. A pre-registered results template: told apart at O24 — a template with the SAME/CHANGED test written into it before the run would have forced the rule into the open instead of letting the graded agent supply it.
whole_checks.rivals_note: Where a rival cannot be told apart by any change on the current list, the honest report is that they are one method at this level, and the finer question is recorded as new.

No change in this case; clarification is not itself a changed verdict" on the O36 and O45 rows. overall.summary: The two-stage pattern is a sound checking pattern carrying the name of a finding pattern, and the gap between those two is where its trouble is. As a check it works and the returns show it working: Stage 1 put an identifier on every verdict, Stage 2 checked 119 quotations, and I confirmed by hand that all 43 file-10 quotations resolve verbatim in the authority. The split earned its keep, narrowly: it caught one over-marked row (O24) and one over-marked card (O52), which a single agent building its own fix card would have carried forward. But three parts pull the finding capacity out of it. The instruction names, in the pasted part, the two rows the round exists to find, and Stage 1 returned exactly those two out of 52, which the project's own Lesson 50 predicts. The auditor is instructed to print Stage 1's verdict before writing its own and says plainly it was not blind, so 19-of-19 agreement on both verdict columns is one reading read twice. And the audit's sample and summary lists are both conditioned on Stage 1's flags, so the pattern can subtract findings and has never added one. The one real finding of the round, Derivation 3's claim outrunning its proof, was produced by the single-stage S70 round before the split and was corroborated by an outside reader working from file 10 alone; the two-stage round confirmed it and reduced two findings to one. The repairs are small and nearly all positive in wording: strike the naming sentence, reverse the print order, make the sample unpredictable and shape-based, and give the audit a heading where it can report a change Stage 1 missed.

rivals.question_frozen: Does the two-stage pattern - Stage 1 reads the theory bare against 52 fixed case cards with an identifier on every verdict, Stage 2 audits that return row by row against the sources and builds the fix card and draft list from what survives, and Claude then reads both and determines - make sense as a way of finding what is wrong with the theory? Frozen over the rounds the record shows it used or planned for (S72, run and returned; S76, written and packed), against the theory as it stands in file 10 and as rewritten in file 11, with the owner's standing choices held fixed (push to main only, a fresh agent per step, returns held unchanged, zips, Claude determines). Three things are asked and all three answered: whether each part does inside the run what the instruction says it does, and whether the S72 returns show it doing so; whether the pattern can fail a wrong theory and pass a right one, with a route by which a wrong theory gets reported wrong rather than absorbed by a reading, a PARKED file or a held-back list; and whether each part is held in place by a job, so that swapping a part for its near neighbour breaks something.

whole_checks.catch_alls: Six, with their gauges. PARKED: gauge is the list; empty in both returns, and nothing asks whether a zero means the pass is too easy, which the project's own Lesson 35 trap says to ask. "Held back by the audit": gauge is the list; it fired once, on O24, with the reason stated and a trap warning against reading it as rejection - the best-made catch-all here. SILENT: gauge is the live-row count in the report's heading (4); it absorbed eight rows this round and the count has read the same for four rounds, so a theory whose fault is muteness would be recorded as a steady reading, not a defect; S76 Part 1 does at least ask, for each of the eight, whether file 11 now names the declared input. REVISED ONLY: gauge is the count, nine rows; bounded and working. UNRECOVERED: 32 rows since log 41, correctly refused an invented mark ("UNRECOVERED - no mark invented", 32 times) and correctly kept out of the NONE count, but they sit outside every gauge the project reads. "Every fifth of the rest": 33 rows unaudited, named honestly in the manifest and in S75, but the same 33 every round.
whole_checks.change_list_gaps: The same 52 cases every round, written by the same author, who is also the author of the instruction, the prediction and (by S76) the theory revision. The same reading rules, supplied by the agents rather than the instruction. Both stages from the same model family. The same deterministic audit sample. No round has added a case aimed at making a clause read CHANGED, or a quotation read DIFFERS, or the fix card's restatement fail. No round has run the thoughtful person's verdict hidden. And the largest gap ahead: file 12 (S77) removes the provenance notions - the three histories of a transport, the genesis attack - that most of the 52 cases are about (O11, O15 to O19, O28 to O34, O40 to O44, O49), so a case set that never changes is about to lose contact with the theory it tests. The record is honest that file 12 is under no round.
whole_checks.direction: Forward inside a row, backward at the level of the round. Inside a row it genuinely runs from the theory to a verdict: the auditor quotes the passage and works its own reading, and I confirmed the passages are real. At the level of the round it runs from the result the author expects: S72's instruction names the two rows before the agents look, and S76's pack carries Claude's own determination (build.py line 47 puts S75 into the S76 Stage 1 pack) plus the instruction's prediction plus the previous agent's column-3 verdicts to quote rather than rederive.
whole_checks.flip: Split the flip in two, because the pattern answers them differently. Had file 10 overclaimed - said more than its proof gives - the run would have reported it, and did: column 6 asks what in the bare version gives the wrong verdict, quoted, and O48's entry reads "The bare claim asserts a differently valued survivor at every unseen pair, while the proof's 'any other admitted relation' does not establish one in this population; this is an overclaim and internal tension, not SILENT." Exactly one row of 52 records such a disagreement. Had file 10 underclaimed - been simply mute on a family of questions, as it is on dividing credit and on "mostly" - the run reports silence, not wrongness: eight rows come back SILENT, the determination calls them places where "the theory declares an input", and the gauge that is supposed to measure this has read the same value for four rounds. So the pattern is built to catch a theory saying too much and records a theory saying too little as a declared input.
whole_checks.hidden_answer: Yes, in four places, and one of them cuts both ways. The instruction names O24 and O48 before the run. Column 2, the thoughtful person's verdict, is printed beside the theory's verdict, so the reader can read the answer off the target; 41 of 52 rows come back "No disagreement". The S76 Stage 1 pack holds S75, the previous returns and the column-3 verdicts to quote. And the forcing case itself, O48, was written by Claude against R2 J's own phrase "admitted-class and realizability qualifications", so the case that shows the qualification is needed was built from the qualification. That last charge is not decisive: O47 was written the same way from another J phrase and came back SAME, and an outside reader reached the same conclusion about Derivation 3 from file 10 alone (log S73), which is the one piece of genuinely independent evidence in the record - and it came from outside this pattern.
whole_checks.jobs_origin: Given by the owner: the split into testing and audit, Claude reading both and determining (S7). Fixed by the owner and not tested here: a fresh agent per step (S5), push to main only and edit nothing outside the folder (S6), returns held unchanged, zips, positive wording (decision 20). Added by Claude: the 52-case set and its verdicts, the identifier on every verdict, the sampling rule, the frozen prediction (S76), the coverage gauge, the three draft lists, the fix card's six fields. Added by me, and so holding nothing until someone else agrees they are real jobs: that the audit should be able to add a finding and not only subtract; that the thoughtful person's verdict should be hidden from the reader on a sample; that the case set should include cases written by someone other than the author of the theory version under test.
whole_checks.parts_origin: Fitted: the case set, tuned round by round on what the previous round's coverage named, and by S76 the theory itself is fitted to it. Built, each against a named failure, and these are the pattern's best parts: the identifier rule (from log 57, where two "earlier version" quotations turned out absent from file 10), the quotation check (same failure), the near-case discipline (from Lesson 35, the gauge that read zero in 32 rows), the fix card's six fields (from log 30), the frozen prediction (from S70's question, how close is a next draft). Asserted: "every fifth", the definitions of SAME, CHANGED and SILENT, and the treatment of 19-of-19 agreement as reason to trust the unaudited 33.
whole_checks.pulls: A fresh agent with no memory against a pack that must carry every earlier round: the S76 Stage 1 pack is 65 files, about 285,000 words of earlier returns against a 7,880-word theory, and the returns show the agent inheriting rather than rederiving ("mechanically recounted rather than independently re-audited row by row"). Freshness gives way. Exactness against the positive-wording rule: the instructions cannot say "do not read column 2 first" - but they can say "work your own reading and print it, then print Stage 1's column", so this pull is resolvable and the record has not tried. Audit sampling against cost: cost wins, 33 of 52 rows unaudited, and the honest naming of that in the manifest is the compensation. A case set that never changes against a theory that changes each round: by S76 the theory is fitted to the cases, and by S77 the theory has dropped what most of the cases are about. Checking against authoring: Stage 2 writes the fix card it will not be audited on. And one nobody has looked at: Stage 1 is told "A second agent will audit what you return", and its rows are heavily hedged ("this does not settle every general coarse-grounding dispute"), which makes DISAGREE harder to earn. Unknown; the test is a run with that sentence removed.
whole_checks.rivals: Six, each with the change that tells it from the two-stage pattern. (1) The single-stage S71 it replaced: the change is who builds the fix card. It told, narrowly - Stage 2 moved O24 from CHANGED to SAME and O52 to placed-by-H64, and a single agent would have carried both into the draft list. But the finding itself, Derivation 3, was produced by the single-stage S70 round, so the split confirmed rather than found. (2) Two independent testers with a tiebreak: the change is whether the second reader sees the first's answer. Here it does, by instruction, and says so; so correlated error passes, and the 19-of-19 agreement cannot be told from one reading read twice. What the pattern buys instead, and blind testers could not, is a check on identifiers, quotations and mark discipline - which is exactly where its two corrections came from. (3) Cases written blind by an outside model with verdicts hidden from the reader: the change is whether the reader can see the target before giving the theory's verdict. Here it can, and 41 of 52 rows come back "No disagreement" in wording that restates column 2 with theory vocabulary attached. (4) The audit run by a different model family: the change is shared blind spots. Both agents adopted the same non-instructed reading of CHANGED, so the load-bearing definition in this round is one the model family supplied, not one the instruction did. (5) A human adjudicator on disputed rows: the change is who resolves the one place the two stages disagreed. Claude resolved it by attributing to the instruction a rule the instruction does not contain, in the direction of fewer findings. (6) A pre-registered results template filled before the run: the change is whether the criterion for CHANGED exists before anyone marks a row. This is the sharpest rival, because S76 shows the project already has the part - and it is a separate part from the split. Single stage plus a written definition of CHANGED would have caught O24 too, at a fraction of the 53,492 words Stage 2 cost. The honest report is that the split and the pre-registration are near neighbours for the job the split is credited with, and the pre-registration is cheaper.
